speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERIES OF PROVINCIAL PARLIAMENTARIANS
speechtext:
May I be allowed to bring to the attention of hon. members the presence in the Speaker's gallery and the Senate gallery of a very distinguished group of fellow parliamentarians from all parts of Canada. These parliamentary colleagues have come to Ottawa to attend during the week the first seminar on parliamentary procedure and practice organized by the Canadian branch of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association. The participants include the Speakers from British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland and they are representative of the provincial legislative assemblies and the legislative councils of the two territories.
On behalf of hon. members I extend a very warm welcome to our distinguished visitors and fellow parliamentarians, and express the wish that their attendance at this seminar will be useful for them and for us and also for the institution of parliament.

MOVEMENT TO EXPORT MARKETS-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to propose a motion under Standing Order 43. This matter is of urgent and pressing necessity and has to do with the delivery hold-up in getting western grain off the farms and into the export markets. As a result, Canada's export trade commitments to foreign buyers are endangered while some grain farmers may suffer financial losses because they are prevented from delivering their grain for sale at present higher prices. With consent I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Horner):
That this House recommends that the subject matter of this motion be forthwith referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture and that the appropriate officials of the Canadian National Railways, the Canadian Pacific Railways, the Wheat Board and the Canada Grains Commission appear before the committee and that, as soon as possible after investigation, the committee report its findings and recommendations to this House.

speechtext: In view of the offer by Mr. Getty, the Alberta Minister of Intergovernmental Affairs, to make available to the province of Quebec 100,000 barrels of oil a day, may I ask the minister what arrangements have been made for delivering that quantity of oil to Quebec? speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in what I think ought to be one of the most important debates that has ever occurred in this House of Commons, namely the debate on Bill C-132. During the few moments at my disposal I do not propose to discuss some of the items examined so eloquently by other members of my party, such as the fact that the bill is entirely negative, that the bill is for the first time, as far as I know, introducing legislation where to a high degree we are to be governed in this country by men instead of by law, or the fact that there is no positive introduction of measures to encourage ownership by Canadians of the resources of this country. Rather I want to direct the attention of the House for a few moments to the general nature of the bill, particularly to the importance of the amendments introduced by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay).
The fact of the matter is that this bill, cannot be given proper consideration because we must consider it outside the framework of any definition on the part of the government of what economic policy this country is going to follow in the future, indeed even outside the framework of a policy for the present time. This makes an assessment of the bill almost impossible.
I am not suggesting that the bill should be debated in terms of the traditional goals of economic policymaking we know so well, namely the goal of full employment, relative price stability, less regional disparity of income and more equitable distribution of income among all Canadians.
The question raised, but not examined by the legislation, a question that is so important, is what direction are we going to take in our general philosophy with respect to economic policymaking in the Canadian economy? I was distressed to hear the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) say in response to a question today that the economy is now operating at close to its full capacity, and this at the same time as we have a 5.8 per cent unemployment rate in this nation; indeed, in some parts of the country the rate is
10	per cent. I do not know whether or not the Minister of Finance suggests that the structure of the Canadian economy has changed so much that we must now accept the proposition that if we are to have the economy operating at the government's definition of full capacity we shall have to accept an unemployment rate of 5V4 per cent or some figure of this sort, a totally unacceptable rate. It seems to have escaped the notice of the minister that this is the highest unemployment rate of any industrialized country in the world at the present time. However, it does illustrate the need to examine whether the foundations of current economic policymaking are appropriate. Where is this country going to go during the next quarter of a century? Do we have to have high unemployment, inflation, regional disparities as a continuous situation?
During the course of this century we have had two basic patterns of development in Canada. First, until world war
11	we had the triangular trade pattern with which we are all familiar. We shipped our raw materials and other products to the British Empire and used our surplus exchange to buy manufactured goods from the United States. Then, after world war II there was a basic shift in

November 13, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act philosophy concerning the management of the Canadian economy, and our policy moved to what I would call in shorthand terms "continentalism". This continentalism was not unusual given the fact that we are so close to the United States, and that there were changes in the rest of the world which made it difficult for the Canadian economy to develop through dependence on Imperial preferences. Moreover, we needed capital to develop the economy.
During this "continentalist" period there has been growth in the Canadian economy, but it has been very uneven and erratic. We have had high unemployment and deep recessions during much of the period, and we are now experiencing a rapid increase in the rate of inflation, one of the most rapid rates of any country in the world. Has our performance been the result of this basic philosophy? The question is worth examining because one result of our policy of continentalism has been that our policymaking has been inextricably linked to policymaking in the United States. Indeed, one could argue that we in this country today are not able to have an independent economic policy.
The degree of inter-relationship with the United States at the present time is clear to all. When that country had a balance of payments crisis and introduced measures to solve it, their decision to devalue caused a devaluation of the Canadian dollar which contributed to the high rate of inflation in this country. When the United States decided to introduce an interest equalization tax, what was our response? To rush down to Washington to try to be exempted from that interest equalization tax. When the DISC program was introduced in the United States, what was our response? To rush down to Washington to see whether we could be exempted from that. The reason I mention these examples is to indicate that the net result of the policy we have followed since the end of world war II has culminated in the result that we are now restricted in making decisions respecting economic policymaking in this country which are independent of decisions that are made in the United States.
I suggest that the debate that we have had on this issue in the last week or so should really revolve around this fundamental question: Are we going to have a change in our attitude toward continentalism? We have now reached a period in the history of Canada when we have to assess this question very carefully and effectively, because the premises on which Canada entered into this kind of policymaking have changed. When the Canadian government decided after world war II that this was the policy in the best interests of the country, the decision was based on the assumption that the U.S. dollar would be a strong currency on international exchanges, that the United States economy would remain strong in the world throughout the 20th century, and that there would be continuing surplus of raw materials throughout the world.
These assumptions may no longer be valid, Mr. Speaker. The United States dollar is no longer a strong world currency. Indeed, it is a currency that has enormous problems associated with it. The U.S. economy has had an endless amount of trouble. So as far as Canada is concerned, basing economic policy on what is done in the

United States may not necessarily lead to the best development of the Canadian economy in the future.
The difficulty about this bill is that it does not provide any indication of what the government's position is on this issue. It does not indicate whether or not the government realizes that the net result of the policy that we have followed for the last 25 years may have caused us to lose a great deal of sovereignty in the field of economic policymaking something which is fundamental to any country that wants to pursue its own goals and to develop its own destiny.
The bill does not deal with investments in unrelated enterprises or with the problem of using retained earnings for investment in other enterprises in tbe Canadian economy. In fact, the bill deals only with new capital investment, something which I am sure the minister will agree has been anything but significant during the last two or three years. In many ways the bill is, in a sense-and I use the word with care-a somewhat fraudulent piece of legislation because it implies that it is dealing with a problem with which it does not deal at all. It does not deal with the question of the takeover of firms by existing subsidiaries operating in the Canadian economy at the present time which has been the major cause of the increase in foreign investment in Canada today.

I certainly have. Similarly, it is hard to assess the intention of the framers of the bill because the bill is not placed in the framework of some type of industrial strategy for the nation as a whole. Is the reason for the bill to strengthen the industrial sector so there will be more employment brought about in manufacturing? If the bill is designed to increase manufacturing employment in Canada, and if that is what it is designed to do, how will it accomplish this? If it is designed to bring about more independence in economic policy making in Canada, in formulation of tax policy and monetary policy as well as exchange rate policy, the bill will have no effect.
This bill will do absolutely nothing about the fundamental problems in the Canadian economy or the critical question of economic sovereignty in Canada at the present time. To suggest that it will is misleading. This bill does not tell us anything about the basic belief of this government as to how the Canadian economy must be developed
November 13, 1973

in the rest of the century. It is simply another ad hoc measure, because it is not set within the framework of an industrial strategy for Canada.
One cannot be astonished that many provinces are upset over a bill which is so vague that they cannot be sure of its intentions. That is why the amendment brought forward by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) is so important.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Which one?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: He has put forward several.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Let me say why it is so important and so worthy of consideration. The amendment provides the minister with a great opportunity to make a major breakthrough in economic policy-making for better operation of the economy. The fact is that we have not been able to reduce substantially regional disparities in Canada. If one looks at the statistics he will see that even with the large operations under DREE our regional disparities are great. Surely, it cannot be surprising that people in the Atlantic provinces, and some of the other areas, are distressed at a bill of this kind. The nature of this bill suggests that one of the important things for them, namely new investment, may well be limited.
Given the unemployment rates in these areas, an unemployment rate today in the Atlantic provinces of approximately 10 per cent, how can the minister tolerate such a situation? How can he tolerate the highest unemployment rate of any industrial country in the world? How can the minister bring in a piece of legislation when the people of these areas are so concerned about this bill they are afraid it will make their problems even worse? The amendment which was introduced provides an opportunity to bring the provinces into the making of decisions which affect them so much?
One has to admit that broad-gauged economic policy making in Canada, using a broad brush in fiscal and monetary policy, has not solved our regional problem. So what we should be talking about in terms of economic policy making, is the whole question of how we are going to bring in and use the input of the provinces in developing national economic policy.
I am suggesting to the minister that, by accepting this amendment, he has a tremendous opportunity to make a first step in a positive direction. There is no question that in the future we will have to change the way in which monetary policy operates, that we will have to interrelate the making of fiscal policies by the provincial and federal governments, if we are going to achieve Canada's potential. We have to consider such issues because the way we have been doing things in the past has not worked.
We cannot ask a part of Canada to live with 10 per cent unemployment. This is immoral, it is improper and certainly an ineffective use of our resources. We must try to do something different, and I am pleading with the minister to take a hard, long look at this possibility. If he can
Foreign Investment Review Act develop, through the use of this bill, a vehicle by which we can really create input by the slow-growth provinces in the development and formulation of policy so that we really have federalism working, and the provinces feel they have an input which is being considered by the federal government in the development of policy, then we will have moved a considerable degree in the direction of the way in which economic policy must be made in Canada in the future. Our methods in the past have not worked. Surely, what we want to do now is find a new mechanism for solving regional problems, and the minister has a vehicle if he accepts the amendment. It is not my suggestion that provinces opt out. It is not in any way weakening the bill. In fact, I suggest the amendment is making it stronger, and is making it more effective.
What the bill does now in terms of the over-all problem of foreign investment in Canada is not very significant. By accepting this amendment this minister will have the opportunity of working out administrative procedures and setting a whole new direction in economic policy making in this country which will effectively relate the work of the central government with the work of the provinces, and this is essential if we are to find solutions to the economic problems of the nation.
I see my time is nearly up, Mr. Speaker, but we must recognize that the Canadian economy has been operating far below its potential. There are probably many reasons for this that one can put forth, including the truncation of our manufacturing segment because of a high degree of foreign ownership and the fact it has been developed in such a way that Canadian firms are not involved to the degree they might be in research, development and so forth. These reasons have all been brought up in the debate. But surely another reason Canada's economy is operating below potential is that we are not organized or structured to make effective policy.
I want to leave this one suggestion with the minister, and I make it with the greatest respect and with all the emphasis I can. By accepting the amendment and bringing the provinces into the discussions in an effective fashion he can lay a foundation which can be a guide for the development of other economic policy in Canada in the future. If we fail to adopt that course, we will not do anything about the question of foreign investment and we will have discontented provinces. The bill will have missed a great opportunity. I really urge the minister to accept the amendment. He must want it. He cannot possibly be content with the way things have happened in the past. I do not think we should miss the opportunity provided by the amendment of the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) to provide provincial participation. I say through you, Mr. Speaker, to the minister that this would be really a start, a new direction, in economic policy making in this country which must come because the past broad gauged policies have not worked. Now is the time for a new start in economic policy making.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak after the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) whom I want to congratulate for taking a somewhat belated interest in the passing of this bill, but he does seem to show some knowledge of it.

I should like to indicate that the hon. member, indeed, is not contemplating the bill in its full force and effect, because surely most of the points he brought to the attention of the minister have been brought to the minister's attention on previous occasions by members of his own party even before the preparation of this particular legislation. I suggest that the aims the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) is seeking would be best given effect by the provisions in the bill as it stands. I would refer to clause 2, subclause (2)(e) which contains an express provision for discussion of the items that are given importance by the provinces. This subclause reads as follows:
In assessing, for the purposes of this Act, whether any acquisition of control of a Canadian business enterprise or the establishment of any new business in Canada is or is likely to be of significant benefit to Canada, the factors to be taken into account are as follows:
Then, they are enumerated. Paragraph (e) reads as follows:
the compatibility of the acquisition or establishment with national industrial and economic policies, taking into consideration industrial and economic policy objectives enunciated by the government or legislature of any province likely to be significantly affected by the acquisition or establishment.
There is no doubt that of the five considerations that are to be taken into account by the minister and by the cabinet one of the five-and there are only five-is the question of policy suggestions enunciated by the provinces. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that these provisions will be effective but that proposals contained in the amendment would bring about the development of an auction system regarding foreign investment in Canada. Surely Nova Scotia, the province from which the mover of the amendment comes, is interested in new investment regardless of its origin. Surely, Nova Scotia government would be approached by the applicant or potential investor in order determine whether or not that particular province would support an application to the federal government and what its specific contribution would be relating to that particular investment.
In this way we would avoid the necessity of every province in the Maritimes having to be advised of this particular potential investment which cause them to start saying, "me first". One province would offer better terms than another and so on. The investor would be placed in the position where his intentions were no longer confidential. He would be involved in the political arena at the outset in respect of which province would get that investment. I believe this is where the real danger lies. The applicant would not benefit from the advice of one area in which he wished to place his investment; indeed, he would be faced with competition between several areas.

I suggest that the amendment is quite explicit in some respects and very vague in others. It reads in part as follows:
A copy of the notice-
That includes the whole kit and kaboodle.
-shall be sent by the Agency forthwith by registered mail to the province or provinces likely to be significantly affected ...
I repeat "significantly". Mr. Speaker, we know the nature of investment in Canada and the nature of the corporate entities in Canada. I defy any member here to indicate an interest which is likely to be purchased by a foreign investor which is not operative in the majority of the provinces of Canada. If someone is interested in purchasing that particular interest, the government would have to notify each province which would be significantly affected by that purchase. I suggest to the hon. member for Don Valley, through you, Mr. Speaker, that by advising each and every province we would find ourselves involved in a multi-faceted discussion and auction between these various provinces. That is the point which creates the greatest difficulty for me in the proposal made in this particular amendment.
The other matter which gives me some concern is that there some areas of Canada which need the protection of the federal government in respect of the provincial government.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman who just intervened knows something about the auction. I congratulate him for protecting that particular mode of sale. I respect the auctioneering process. Although it is as he
November 13, 1973

states a God-like process, I suggest that in this particular instance it would not work. I regret the aspersions I may have cast. I merely suggest that the auction system, although valid, does not apply in a situation or in a confederation where we wish to nurture co-operation between individual provinces. It is important that individual provinces recognize each other's rights, and also recognize the right of the central government to protect the interests of the whole Confederation rather than only one section.
As I was saying, we still need the protection of the federal government for certain areas of Canada which have been neglected by their provincial governments. I suggest that the bill in its present form will protect northern Ontario, and we will find that the practices of the past will not apply if some company should wish to locate in that area.
I feel it is very difficult to comprehend the attitude taken by the Conservative party in this instance. They have been chastising the government, and the thrust of their contributions has been that the government should not protect its jurisdictional responsibilities. Evidently they support the position of the province of Alberta in the matter of supplying energy to the whole of Canada. They espouse the attitude taken by that particular province in confronting the federal government. Their position is that there should be a confrontation between the provinces which might want to have investment within their own boundaries and the federal government which is attempting to make a just distribution of industry throughout Canada. They take issue with that idea and say the federal government should not consider what the provinces want and should not protect its jurisdictional responsibilities, but rather should throw the ball into the provincial park so that the provinces can confront each other and confront the federal government in attempting to arrive at a decision.
I find it very difficult to understand why a federal party such as the Conservative party should support the idea of the decentralization of the federal power to such an extent. I find it most unjustifiable, especially when about two months ago they were saying that the federal government should impose wage and price controls, knowing that this would necessitate consultation with the provinces because the federal government does not have jurisdiction to impose wage and price controls without the consent of the provinces. No mention was ever made of any consultation with the provinces on that subject.
Again, with reference to the energy situation, when the Conservative party was espousing a national energy policy and telling the government that it does not have a national energy policy, which they wanted forthwith, no indication was made of any necessity for consultation with the provinces. They did not consider, of course, that there was a national energy policy. Perhaps it was not satisfactory to the opposition, but it was there. Therefore, we have a considerable amount of difficulty in accepting the sincerity of the opposition. The Progressive Conservative party is now indicating that there should be confrontation with reference to foreign ownership at the time when there is some indication that they do not favour the
Foreign Investment Review Act limitation of foreign investment in Canada. We see quite clearly from the speeches of members of that party that they are not really interested in the control of foreign ownership. I am suggesting that they are using this amendment to create some sort of dissension within the House so that the bill might be defeated.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today, in discussing the foreign investment review bill, I want to talk about love and hate, fact and fiction, common sense and foolishness. During the past week or so in this House all these factors have come into play. If I may be a little partisan for a moment, perhaps I should say that the love, the facts and the common sense in relation to foreign investment in Canada have been displayed by members of the Progressive Conservative party-the only political party in Canada with elected members from all ten provinces-and the negative aspects I have mentioned have come from either the members across the floor or to my extreme left.
As my good friend from Crowfoot, Alberta, mentioned a day or so ago, Canadian ownership in business and industry is like motherhood; it is desired and it is respected. In a perfectly balanced world, if Canada had a much larger population, if geographical factors had been different, perhaps even if history had been different, foreign ownership in Canada might not be the controversial subject it is today. Then again, perhaps if geography had been different, if history had been different, if our population had been much larger, perhaps Canada would not be the great and marvellous country it is today. You cannot have everything, Mr. Speaker. You can try to have the best of both worlds, but you do not always get it. Actually, I think Canada has come closer than any other country to having the best of both worlds, and I think that with a little common sense we just might achieve it.
I say "common sense" because I recognize that, rightly or wrongly, foreign ownership in Canada has become both a controversial and a pressing subject. The New Democrats to my left, the party in Canada which is not happy unless it is kicking our closest neighbour south of the border, favour the ending of all foreign investment in Canada right now. Well, if we did that, many other countries would be very happy because it would mean that the United States would have to look elsewhere to invest its money. With investment you get jobs, lots of jobs. Most countries want to increase employment. They hate to see their citizens out of work. So, they welcome more foreign investment.
Some people in Canada still welcome foreign investment. In fact, Nova Scotia premier Gerald Regan, a Liberal, becomes upset when we talk about restricting investment in this country. He has good reason to be. The Maritimes are a have-not group of provinces with high unemployment rates, and Premier Regan knows he cannot say no to investment that will give more jobs to the residents of his province. Even though I am not a Liberal, I would like to see Mr. Regan in this House of Commons now giving his views on foreign investment. It might interest the government and it might interest the New Democrats who have failed to elect even one federal member of parliament from the Maritimes. They do not have even one from an area which, with its economic

November 13, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act problems, you would think would be a natural hunting ground for them.
Now, I have mentioned the foolishness of a small but highly vocal group which says: Let us end all foreign investment, let us throw out all the Yanks. That is foolishness, and I am sure that the premiers of Manitoba, British Columbia and Saskatchewan-all NDP premiers who have gone to the United States and spoken about the need for investment in their provinces-know how foolish it is to want to turn away that money and to let investors and jobs go elsewhere.
What I think is needed when it comes to discussing foreign investment and guidelines for foreign investment is common sense. I understand that 100 years or more ago there were people in the United States who worried about British investment in their country. Time has shown them to have been wrong. I guess it has also shown them that without that initial amount of foreign investment, the U.S. economy could never have expanded at the rate it has.
I think perhaps if we imagined a Canada in which not one U.S. cent, one English pound or one West German mark had been invested over the past 100 years, we would see that we would have a pretty sad country. Canadians did not have the money. We needed outside help, and we got it. We took that help for 100 years. Now, we start to say, "Go away; we don't want you any more." That is a strange attitude, Mr. Speaker. It is a strange attitude because if a foreign corporation wants to build an industry in one country, and that country says no, then it will simply build the plant in another country that says, "Yes, we need the jobs you can give us. We need them for our young people. We need your industry because it will contribute to our tax base and perhaps even build up our export trade."
I realize there are some problems with foreign investment. I realize that profits from some foreign-owned industries, not only U.S. but Japanese, British and West German, flow out of this country at an alarming rate. And so I think we have to have some regulations, some guidelines, and some rules, but not rules so tough that no one will locate here. Let us have some common sense. In fact, I think we have some common sense in the bill before the House. I will be interested to see it go through the committee stage and get some input from outside, some refining. But I do not think the bill as such, or the government as such, is tackling the problem in a realistic way. It seems to me that instead of restricting, instead of taking negative attitudes, we should encourage and take positive measures to deal with our foreign ownership problem. We should try to have the best of two worlds.
As I said before, Mr. Speaker, I do not believe we are in a position to turn down employment creating opportunities. At the same time, I realize that a country on the move has to guide its own destiny. I think we can have the jobs and also guide our own destiny if we approach the matter properly. Suppose that foreign investment in this country continued to grow at the rate that it has over the past decade or so, but that Canadian investment and ownership grew at a rate perhaps 5 per cent to 10 per cent higher than of investment by United States investors. It seems to me

that in this case, as U.S. and other foreign investment continued to grow, because Canadian investment and ownership would be growing at a rate 5 per cent to 10 per cent higher, then in a certain period of time Canadian ownership in the various industries would match foreign ownership. Then, if we could maintain the relative rates of growth, it would far surpass outside ownership. We would still get the foreign investment, still get the new jobs for our young people, but as Canadian ownership grew at a greater clip, the actual percentage of foreign ownership would slowly fall. And I stress slowly. We would have the best of two worlds. We would still get the investment and the jobs, but over a period of time we would gain the upper hand. I repeat that we would have the best of two worlds.
How can this be done? The weapon, if I can call it that, seems to me to be taxation. We should change our taxation policies so that they offer more incentives to Canadians- just enough to give Canadian businessmen and entrepreneurs an edge without scaring away outside investors. This certainly is not the case now. In the oil and gas industry, for instance, foreign investors putting their money into high-risk oil and gas exploration in Canada get more incentives and more taxation writeoffs than Canadians receive. It is a strange situation. And I note that the NDP, which only managed to gather some 17 per cent of the vote in the 1972 federal election and elected only 31 out of 264 members, but which is now the power behind the throne, views with alarm foreign domination of the Canadian oil and gas industry.
Why doesn't it do something about it? Why doesn't the NDP force the Liberal government to give Canadians the same taxation advantages that Canada gives to foreign investors? Because, as usual, the NDP can't see the forest for the trees, and competition scares the NDP. It does not feel it is equal to the task so it avoids the fight, and avoids innovation. The NDP and, I am afraid the Liberal government, avoid giving Canadian businessmen and entrepreneurs the encouragement and inventives they need to give them that little spurt which will put Canadians ahead just enough to control their own destiny without scaring off anyone else.
I remember that during the 1972 election campaign our leader proposed a revolutionary plan that would allow Canadians to invest up to $5,000 a year in a small Canadian-owned business and, at the same time, get an equivalent amount of deferred income for tax purposes. It was quite a plan. It was designed to allow the average Canadian, whether he had $500 or $5,000 to invest each year, to put it in a small Canadian-owned business and so help it expand. The government, under the Progressive Conservatives, would then allow him to defer paying income tax on that investment until he sold out his holding. That is what I call one positive step to increase Canadian ownership in this country, a positive not a negative step, a method by which more, not fewer, jobs would be created, and a measure, I might note, that would give more Canadian wage earners the opportunity to enjoy the fruits of the free enterprise system.
Is that idea lost, Mr. Speaker? I do not think so. I do not think so because I believe that sooner or later, perhaps sooner than most people realize, the Progressive Conserva-
November 13, 1973

tives will form a government in this country and will institute such realistic and advanced ideas. We have to, Mr. Speaker, because if we do not we are going to be in a terrible mess.
I was reading in the Financial Post on the weekend, the issue dated November 10, about a small Canadian-owned manufacturing company, Husky Manufacturing and Tools Works Ltd., of Bolton, Ontario. This company wanted to expand its manufacturing operation. What did it find? If found that every major cost and tax involved in the expansion would be higher in Canada than if the company located in the United States. It seems that after the company president, Robert Schad, looked into the matter, he found that his company's after-tax profits from a new manufacturing plant located south of the border rather than in Ontario would be more than double. The figures showed that the Canadian operations would yield an estimated pre-tax profit of $1.2 million, whereas his company would make a profit of almost $2.3 million before tax if the new plant were located just a couple of hundred miles away. So, we have a case of good-bye profits, goodbye jobs. We even force our own entrepreneurs and businessmen to expand their operations outside the country. It seems to me, looking at this particular case, that something is very, very wrong. Common sense tells me that. Let us give our own people the encouragement and incentives they need to invest in Canada. Let us give them all the help they need, because new jobs are too important to throw across the border.
A month or so ago the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who incidentally has alienated the entire province of Alberta and almost all of western Canada and the Mari-times with his strange attitudes and policies, went tripping off to Red China. My comment on that meeting would have been simple. His time would have been better spent in Washington. I cannot help but wonder why the Prime Minister was not trying to make Canadians better liked closer to home. I would have thought there was a more important job to do fixing up relations with our closest neighbour and biggest trading partner, the United States. I submit that instead of visiting Communist China the Prime Minister should have been in Washington, London, Japan and Europe patching up relationships which his government has destroyed. Ask the average Canadian who is his closest friend, and he is not likely to say Red China. He can see things clearer closer to home. It is a pity the right hon. Prime Minister cannot.
So, Mr. Speaker, let us stop kicking our neighbours. Let us stop ignoring our friends. Let us stop creating animosity with those who want to be our friends, and with our own Canadian businessmen. Let us help them create new industries. Let us help them create new jobs. Let us give them the encouragement and incentives they need to make Canadian-owned industries grow, without scaring off people outside our borders who want to invest in our future. I ask the House, where would we be today if we were not rich in resources, and no one wanted to invest in Canada? Let us thank God we have the resources, we have the people wanting to invest in our future. Now, all we need is the same quality to guide these investments that the Canadian businessman exercises in his own day to day operation-common sense. Let us be rational. Let us be
Foreign Investment Review Act fair. Let us be realistic. Let us help Canada grow, not hamper it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I really did not intend to participate at this stage of the debate until I listened to some of my friends across the way. They made me wonder if they really want the bill, particularly the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Hurl-burt). He spoke about things that are not about to happen, such as the possibility of a Progressive Conservative government! What caught my ear and caused me to rise was his reference to the article which appeared in the Financial Post about Husky Manufacturing and Tool Works Limited. Mr. Schad is an entrepreneur. I knew him when he came to this country, a toolmaker from Baden-Baden, Germany. As a matter of fact, I knew his wife before he did but nothing can be read into that!
One should understand the nature of this operation, Mr. Speaker. It is a brilliant operation and Mr. Schad has done a brilliant job. The success which he has enjoyed has been largely the result of his own ingenuity and energy, and I think it is presumptious to say that Canada has made it so difficult for him to operate here that he would be better off if he were to go to the United States. I spoke to him last week about these same tax considerations. Of course, these considerations include DISC and we do not approve of that; it is not in keeping with the international atmosphere that should exist. I do not think we should just lie down to the United States dictates in this respect. We should not forget that many of these companies were built up largely with research and development funds supplied by the government of Canada, and with a great deal of assistance in displaying at exhibitions in Japan, Germany, the United States and other countries.
I think the case that Mr. Schad makes has some merit, but I do not think it is a classic example of the factors that should be considered in deciding our foreign investment policy. One of the interesting facets of our relationship with the United States is that it is taken so much for granted. The fact is that our trade continues to grow and the manufacturing segment of our exports to the United States continues to increase. We do some $30 billion per year of trade with the United States, so I would hardly think that relations with them are being destroyed. Visits to China, the Soviet Union, Asia and other areas of the world where we will find future markets are not counterproductive nor mutually exhaustive. Someone had to take the initiative in establishing the contacts and that was done very well by our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who was followed by leaders of nations greater in size than ours.
When this bill was studied in committee, Mr. Speaker, some members of the Conservative Party talked like nationalists. They know very well that the majority of Canadians support this bill, so while they talked like nationalists they amended like continentalists. I cannot help but feel that their amendments are designed to emasculate the bill.

speechtext:
It is an interesting point of debate, Mr. Speaker. I speak from experience of doing business with many countries in the world, but mostly in the United States and Canada, as well as having a company in the United States.
The point is when you have a rule that the investment be of significant benefit to Canada, you can make a much better deal. You have a bargaining strength there that has a special value because the government has an opportunity to show potential investors how much greater the benefit to Canada will be if they invest in a different way. If there is no such agency investors go wherever they want, of course. If we are able to consult with the provinces, as a screening agency must, the benefits to other parts of Canada can be shown. Those of us from the so-called golden horseshoe are well aware that growth for its own sake is not the answer to everything. Votes are not won in that area by telling people how much bigger the area is to become and how the population is to be increased. If you want to win their votes you tell them how they can enjoy the good life in Edmonton or other places! The fact is that we deal from day to day with the dimensions of investment in matters over which we have very little control. Here we are trying to give the federal government an instrument to encourage investment in the best interests of Canada. But, Mr. Speaker, if I read the amendment correctly, it would give the provinces the power of veto in some cases, and I think this would be extremely unwise.
The industrial strategy to which the hon. member for Don Valley referred does not come by divine revelation, not like tax reform; it comes about by a series of policies in key areas. I suggest that these policies are developing at a rate at which they can be absorbed and discussed with a degree of intelligence in committee and in the House. That could not be done if you tried to impose some master plan from above. Think of what this government has done under regional economic expansion. Of course, it is not perfect but it is the first significant move of any government in our history. This bill will help improve and

strengthen regional expansion and will expand research and development programs. The growth of the Industrial Development Bank, and the restructuring which is about to take place, will be of tremendous value. The establishment of the Canada Development Corporation is another important factor. These are the things that are the matrix of industrial strategy.
As I said, I was constrained to enter this debate because I found my hon. friends opposite straddling the fence, trying to show the nationalist people that they are nationalists but at the same time showing their other friends that they really do not mean it. They do not want this measure to be effective. They do not want to see things changed. That is traditional. That is what we expect. Effectively, the amendment would give veto power to the provinces in many cases and emasculate the bill. The federal government should be in the position to act in the over-all interests of the entire country.
The hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Blais) referred to auctions. I do not want to get into an auction with the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Hurlburt). The fact remains that the provinces, particularly those which are not industrialized, perhaps in anxiety or over anxiety, might make or accept deals which are less favourable. In a recent private arrangement that I had, I found that by simply quoting from the intent of the bill, and some of the amendments to the corporation act, I could make a much more realistic arrangement, and one which certainly was in the best interests of Canada.
I was in New York a week or two ago where I met the head of a multinational corporation. I discussed the arrangements which they accepted, not anxiously but without reluctance, in other countries of the world. I was absolutely astounded. This company does business in virtually every country of the world. Whatever rules there are, they go along with them. They say they cannot afford to do otherwise because if they do not, their competitors will.
What we are proposing is certainly mild compared to countries less buoyant and with less stable governments. We are particularly favoured with a stable government. The opportunities, skills, educational level and resources that exist in this country count very much when investments are made here. If we have some restrictions and provide guidelines in some cases and incentives in others, we can develop greater industry. This will be of great value to Canada and all Canadians. What is important is the nature and quality of these investments and the distribution of them. I do not accept the fact that we should be ungrateful for all the investment we have had in the past. It has been good. However, we are seeing what effect it can have on us.
Many of our major decisions have been distorted by the decision-making location of multinational corporations. We must keep in mind that a lot of these decisions are made by Canadians who are employed by these companies. They think in a head office context which ultimately is not really in our best interest. We must have this opportunity to review these decisions. One example of this is the current oil situation. Had the major oil companies
November 13, 1973

been Canadian owned, the decisions would have been much different. It is true the investment for exploration and development came from multinational corporations. To say we would not have had this industry without that initial foreign investment is a bit of conjecture. I am sure other investors would have been found. However, if we had had regulations, rules and some guidelines for these companies to follow when they started in this country, we would not be boxed in as we are now. This is the time to do something. We cannot do it any sooner.
This is reasonable and fair legislation. It must go through to give us some degree of control over our own destiny. It is going to be of particular value to those parts of the country which in the past have been less favoured economically and, speaking selfishly as a Torontonian, in our best interests because we will see the rest of Canada flourish as well. We flourish only to the extent the rest of Canada flourishes. This is of real importance in the long run. One of our greatest problems in this country is economic disparity. This bill, certainly in concert with regional economic legislation and incentives, will do more for regional economic expansion, bringing industry to parts of Canada that do not have active industry, than anything else we have done.
If we fool around with this bill too much and put too many hedges in it, we will be in danger of limiting its food effects considerably. We must give the screening agency the opportunity to work, to consult with the provinces and work with them. This is an essential part of their job. It is an essential part of the bill. Amendments must not restrict their freedom to operate. If we are going to have a bill and a policy for which the provinces in the long run will thank us, the people who elect us will thank us and, perhaps even more important, our children will thank us.

Foreign Investment Review Act requires is some central reviewing agency which will tell any part of the country whether or not it should have an expansion of industry or a new investment with a modicum of foreign investment. We are to be told, not consulted. This amendment talks about consultation.
The hon. member for York North dared to talk about the oil industry. As a result of the tunnel vision prevalent in the area from which he comes he thinks that if the oil had been developed in a different way, we would not have the problems of today. Let him talk to his financial friends in Toronto. For example, would they have approved or even thought of a pipeline into Montreal three years ago when offshore crude was much cheaper to produce than domestic crude? Is it suggested that the Energy Conservation Board of the Province of Alberta knows not of what it speaks or that all the experience it has collected since 1947 is not worth one tittle by comparison with the newly acquired, unproven judgment of an agency making a recommendation without consultation? There is no word about consultation in this bill. All it says is that the minister, when making his recommendation to the Governor in Council, shall at the same time submit any representations which may have been made by the provinces. In fact, the bill does not require that a notice of an application be sent to a province which has not, in the language of the measure, stated its economic policies. I know this bill, and perhaps that is more than can be said for some of the other hon. members who have sought to support it on this question of consultation.
I want to make it clear that when it comes to the question of being Canadian, I defy anyone on the other side of the House to show that any of us on this side who may be critical of this measure are any less Canadian than they. But they have wrapped around themselves a toga of nationalism and virtue which ill becomes them because of the manner in which they have acted in the past. They remind me of one of my opponents in the last election. He had a Winnebago caravan with half a dozen Canadian flags on the back of it and, on the sides, the famous Liberal slogan "I care". What humbug! What hypocricy! What pretentiousness! Many of the speeches in support of this bill fall into the same category. Of course, we are all concerned.
Does the hon. member for York North pretend that no account is to be taken of decisions of the Alberta Energy Conservation Board, formerly the Energy and Gas Conservation Board, with regard to the quantities of oil to be exported from that province to the rest of Canada, or to the United States? speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps it is my background before I arrived at this House which makes me view Bill C-132 with a great deal of doubt. Throughout the years I spent in the provincial legislature of New Brunswick it seemed as though federal policy made one incursion after another into the rights of the provinces. To me, this bill is equal to any in its imposition of federal government position upon the provincial domain.
While this principle may apply in an important way to that area of Canada which is well developed, where income is above average, where employment opportunities, as has been shown by the figures released on October 20, would very well indicate that the unemployment problem there is by no means as serious as it is in the periphery of Canada, particularly in the provinces of New Brunswick and Newfoundland, and while these areas from Quebec City to Windsor may be able to withstand a lot of unemployment, particularly if investment control is imposed by Ottawa, I submit that there has to be some discretionary power and some provincial input in order that we shall not find ourselves even worse off than at present in under-developed areas of Canada.

November 13, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act
It is with this in mind that I fully support all those amendments which pertain to input by the provinces and guidelines by the provinces regarding investment within their domain. I am not one who is absolutely against the control of foreign investment in Canada. I recognize fully that it is necessary for Canada to have a policy, but this particular policy, as introduced to the House of Commons by the government on your right, Sir, is such that once again it is a patchwork policy which applies only to certain portions of Canada. It bodes very serious hardships for other areas if it is not administered in a very lenient fashion, indeed.
It is never good that a government should be vested with the power by its own legislation to create policy at the whim and pleasure of the government of the day and apply it in locations which it may choose for one reason or another. It is quite possible that reason could pertain to the politics of the government of the day. I say this with no particular accusation against those on your right; I say it as it applies to all governments. There is an inclination by governments to be a little more lenient in areas where the people have been much more favourably impressed by their policies and candidates.
It is with this in mind that I do not like enabling legislation by this or any other government, but suggest that legislation should spell out in detail the policy the government has in mind rather than enabling it to create regulations, to make decisions ad hoc in respect of a particular situation and adjust policy under it on a momentary basis. This is the primary danger of this bill and it is in this field that it infringes mostly on provincial rights.
I think the bill overlooks the relationship of the economy of Canada to the economies of the various regions of Canada. Again, I am going to cite the example I feel is basically the best example. The net income which the agriculture industry of Canada may experience from time to time reflects itself upon the total income of Canada by virtue of the demands of the agricultural community as it expands its plant and spends its money for improvement in its operations and thus makes demands upon the national income in an expansive sort of way. What applies to agriculture, which is today a small percentage of our total economy, will apply equally to developments on the periphery as well as developments in the centre.
If it is possible to create a financial climate in which development will take place in the Atlantic area, as an example, it will most certainly be reflected in a very important way in the more highly industrialized areas of the rest of Canada. It seems to me that the policy of the government should be that where it is possible investment shall be directed to those areas of Canada where the economic structure is the weakest. I do not say this should happen on the basis of, let us do something for New Brunswick, Newfoundland, Saskatchewan and so forth, but rather that there are products and commodities which lend themselves to economic production outside the basically industrialized areas of Canada.
Perhaps the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) epitomized best the feeling I have when he expressed himself as feeling there might be cause for resignation from Cabinet if heavy water was not produced in his

province. It was amazing that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Dube) from New Brunswick did not join him in chorus because certainly heavy water is a commodity on which transportation costs have very little influence in respect of the total cost at the point of use. It is, therefore, a product which could and should be developed by Canada in areas where economic expansion is required. This is a case for the development of a national economic policy, not for the development of a patchwork quilt, and not for the allocation of a heavy water plant to an area of Canada which is already more industrialized than many others. It is in this field that the government could play an important part.
It has recently been announced that there are no additional plans for a heavy water plant in New Brunswick. This takes away the economic base and employment opportunity, as well as a tax base, for both Canada and New Brunswick which would be most favourable in that area. It would provide for energy requirements which, in turn, would create further employment and perhaps further subsidiary development around the heavy water plant. It was with deep regret that I read the news report this morning that it has been pretty well finalized that New Brunswick shall not receive the initial allocation of a heavy water plant.
Let me repeat that it is not my feeling that we should be without a policy in respect of Canadian ownership of Canadian resources and Canadian industry. I feel very strongly on this, and have felt that way for a good many years. Perhaps in my initial year at college during the study of economics it became a matter of some serious concern to me that the flow of cash from Canada in respect of dividends, interest charges and so on as a result of our dependence upon foreign currencies for our civic, provincial and federal development as well as our industrial development was draining away Canadian opportunity. This is no new, snap decision that there should be a national policy for us to obtain owernship or our own community.
However, it is my opinion that this cannot be done with drastic enabling legislation of this type, a type which enables the government to make a decision on a political basis rather than on the basis of the economic necessities of the area concerned. It is very interesting to note that virtually the whole of the first part of the last issue of the Financial Post carries several items to indicate that Canada has not created a climate in which Canadian money is particularly interested in development and expansion within our borders. It pointed out three specific additional cost factors for one concern, which exceeded the cost factors in respect of this plant if it were to expand outside our border. The first of the additional costs was the sales tax. The second was the very substantial differential between the income tax structure in Canada and the income tax structure in the United States. The third was the fact that the Government of Canada has not to date been able to negotiate a trade situation in which our products could go to the United States without duties which prohibit their production in Canada.
It is important that we develop the economic climate in Canada whereby Canadian money will reinvest in Canada
November 13, 1973

rather than seek opportunity abroad in more attractive economic climates. We have heard several companies in Canada criticized because of their increased charges to the consumers for goods and services. Among these companies, for instance, is the Bell system. I have no quarrel with the Bell system and do not wish to interfere with those who oppose its rates. But it is significant that in the first three-quarters of this year that system has had a tax demand of $33 million higher than the tax demand of one year ago and that this tax demand comes from all levels of government, municipal, provincial and federal. The accumulated increase to date is $33 million for a single corporation in Canada. It is no wonder that subscribers scream when there are applications for rate increases, but if the taxes are to be increased at this rate then I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, there is little recourse to industry but to ask the consumers of these various goods and services to pay more.
This is not the fault of the producer, the service industries or the manufacturers. It is caused by the lack of an economic policy in Canada which would recognize for Canada the need of an internationally competitive economic climate which we lack. It seems to me that the bulk of those who have spoken in strong support of this bill are those who come from the industrialized areas of Canada. Those of us who have the misfortune to live in areas of Canada which are not industrial, those of us who live in the area of Canada where unemployment went up by 2.8 per cent in the last month, those of us who have seen the unemployment rolls increased by 7,000 within one province, those of us in another province who have watched unemployment rise by 1.5 per cent in the last month's statistics are the people who are concerned about the fact that we are about to control investment without any suggestion that there should be special consideration, special input and special participation by the areas which need this.
Let me quote from page 7638 of Hansard from the remarks of the Minister responsible for DREE. He said:
The implication of this are-
He is referring to the economic expansion program, the control and so on.
-first, that it is a commitment on our part to reinforce provincial priorities;
If it is the intention of the government to reinforce provincial priorities, then it should incorporate them in one of the amendments in respect of provincial participation in the decision-making process. Let us go on.
... that is, how a province uses its resources or, in the general scheme of things, how those resources are to be developed is something that the province will need to decide in the first instance. Second, once we have identified a major developmental opportunity on which we are prepared-
Please note that word "prepared".
-to work, the very fact that the federal and provincial governments agree on that and sign an agreement to that effect will, of course, be as strong an assurance as you can get that that enterprise is going to be acceptable within the criteria set down in this bill.
The real problem is that the government of Canada shall make the final decision in respect of priorities within the boundaries of a province concerning what is developed,
Foreign Investment Review Act how it is developed and where the money will come from. This is made very clear by the minister's remarks. Let us take another look. In respect of the provinces and regions of Canada, as recorded again at page 7638, he said:
. . . the provinces are given strong assurance that provincial interests and provincial rights will be taken into account.
If these assurances are, in fact, acceptable to the provinces, then I say incorporate them in an amended bill so that the provinces will in fact see that they have an element of authority in the decision-making process in respect of their own economic development. I might add that the minister took unto himself the opportunity to deny statements he made in the past in respect of the rights of his own province, a province of comparable economic development. There is the implication in his speech that he is very unhappy with the premier of his own province in respect of development in that province. It is implied that he is critical of his political patron who put him where he is today, and it is very doubtful if that political patron were able to speak out in his own defence that this gentleman would be returned to this House of Commons. In his remarks he certainly has abdicated the position which any member from the Atlantic area should take in support of the requirements of that area.
He went on to imply in his speech again that the provinces would come to the lap of the federal government because of the goodies the federal government had to deliver. There is the suggestion that only if the provinces comply with the wishes of the federal government will they have their wishes met in respect of development. This bill puts in the hands of the government of Canada discriminatory powers. It must be recognized that in the Atlantic area, if there is a takeover by a Canadian firm, the process of the removal of employment and earning opportunities begins forthwith. The accounting, the invoicing, the high salaried individuals associated with a firm taken over in the Atlantic area by a central Canadian firm creates additional job opportunities in the high salaried class in that area which I mentioned from Windsor to Quebec city and withdraws from the Atlantic area the executive opportunity which the business would present, very often under foreign management.
It is significant, I think, that the bulk of the industries which have been taken over by Canadian capital have, as a result of these policies, contracted employment opportunities rather than expanded them. It is dangerous for a business to be taken over in any area, but its hope for expansion in the Atlantic area is amplified when the source of funds does not come from central Canadian industry. This is not a condemnation of central Canadian industry; it is merely a recognition of the economic facts of life, such as, that you should have centralized administration, you should expand as best you can within sight of your head office, and you should get the economic structure of your firm as centralized as possible to exercice mass economies for national distribution. This practice has been followed.
The prime example that we can cite, of course, is the takeover by a Canadian firm some years ago of a soap

November 13, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act factory in the town of St. Stephen in my constituency. They took away every single job that was in that industry to central Canada and left the town holding the bag. We can go to the same town where a Canadian operated branch closed. It is Milltown, adjacent to St. Stephen and now incorporated with it. The Canadian corporation in the textile industry was closed down. We can also take a look at the town of Marysville where a similar occurrence took place. These companies closed down after a takeover with central Canadian money; they closed their doors and several hundred jobs were lost to the province.

The business world in Canada has found, for instance, as I have mentioned earlier, that no competitive situation is created in Canada when interest rates are as high as they are and when taxes are as high as they are, for Canadian money spent in this country. The outflow of Canadian currency to foreign fields is something which should be discouraged by government policy and not by government regulation. It should be encouraged by our efforts to negotiate a reasonable tariff structure with many of our world partners. It should be created by an analysis of our income tax structure in Canada, our depreciation structure versus that offered in the competitive field in the world market.
If this bill gave any indication whatsoever that the government of Canada, as it is today, had a program for the development of opportunities for Canadian taxpayers to buy shares or for the creation of an atmosphere in which the international world would be prepared to sell its shares to Canadian participants, this would be a step in the right direction. But no such program has been suggested. The speeches in support of this bill have not been in condemnation of those who have spent money on Canadian development. However, they have in no way encouraged further development. It is quite proper to say that the red tape which has existed in the Ottawa structure has made it most discouraging for any individual to try to undertake such a development, with the assistance of DREE or any other department of government.
It is significant to note that several applicants who were desirous of spending money in Canada for development of Canadian industry decided that this bill was the last blow to their application and, as a result, tens of millions of dollars of potential investment, some in secondary industry, some in the processing industry, have been withdrawn from the Atlantic area. They are not interested in investing in Canada. These instances did not involve processing or manufacturing which exploit our natural resources only but rather relate to secondary manufacturing.

I will not impose upon the privilege extended to me. Let me only say that I deplore the fact that the government has chosen not to assist New Brunswick in the opportunity it had for a heavy water plant. I deplore the fact that it has not recognized and taken advantage of the opportunity to scatter some items of high cost-low weight high value items-throughout Canada so that we could develop them. It is then, and only then, that an act such as this can be productive in Canada for our ownership and at the same time for development. In no way can the Atlantic area share or look forward to sharing equal opportunity in employment or standards of living at its present rate of development. There is great fear and mistrust in respect of the way in which this bill may be administered, and in respect of the potential opportunity which may develop, if judgment is not made with great discretion and in recognition of the employment and development requirements of our area.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a stranger who reads the many speeches made today on Bill C-132 might be pardoned were he to wonder just which
November 13, 1973

party in the House was sponsoring this legislation-surely not the junior partners in this unholy alliance of unhappy bedfellows. The NDP has done nothing but criticize the bill. They say it is too weak; it will not do the job, but it is better than nothing. The Liberals have been distinguished mainly by their silence. Until today, I believe only three Liberals rose to speak on this bill, although they have been somewhat more vocal this afternoon. However, they all have one thing in common. They continually and consistently accuse the Official Opposition of being opposed to any control of foreign investment, which is a deliberate distortion of the facts. Why do they adopt these tactics? It reminds me very very much of the old debating ploy in school circles. When you had a very weak argument which you could not support with facts, the usual tactic was to confuse the issue and ridicule the stand taken by your opponent. This debating ploy seldom worked in school circles, and I suggest it will not fool anyone in this debate,
On the other hand, the position of the Official Opposition has been stated over and over again. It was stated very clearly by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay), in whose name stand two of the amendments on which I wish to speak later. It was stated most eloquently again this afternoon by the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies). Certainly, we want to retain control over our natural resources. Certainly, we recognize the political implications of foreign economic domination. After all this is the party of Macdonald, and we were the first proponents of economic nationalism. We still believe in economic nationalism but in its proper perspective. It is fine to encourage Canadian ownership, but only if it is done within the framework of a broad national industrial policy. But in encouraging economic nationalism let us be very careful that we do not drive away foreign capital from those areas of the country which still need massive infusions of capital, unless we make sure that we replace that foreign capital with Canadian capital, or with some other form of capital investment.
Recently, I read a paper put out by the C.D. Howe Research Institute, prepared by Dr. David Springate, dealing with regional incentives and private investment, in which he gave an assessment of regional incentives offered by DREE. I think it is appropriate at this time to quote briefly from Dr. Springate's paper. It outlines our position very well. It outlines what should be Canada's national industrial policy. He refers to the fact the RDIA program has two subsidiary goals, and then writes;
The final goal is that of encouraging international investment in Canada. The pursuit of this objective confronts two opposing constraints and trends. One is the country's apparent need for such investment. The other is a growing sense of economic nationalism.
Canada traditionally has been a heavy user of foreign capital in the form of both portfolio investment and, more significantly for our purposes, direct investment. The familiar arguments relating to capital need and the extent of foreign ownership will not be repeated here. It is enough to state that one implication of a situation where over half a country's manufacturing capacity is foreign owned is that attraction of foreign investment must continue to take place if a steady expansion in the economy and in the number of jobs is to occur. If foreign owners do not find Canada an attractive place in which to invest (or re-invest), they can withdraw funds and invest elsewhere. Given Canada's need for
Foreign Investment Review Act economic expansion and job creation, the possibility of reduced foreign investment is a prospect that many Canadians find undesirable.
Dr. Springate is not the only one to state this point of view. It was stated clearly by the Premier of Quebec back in January, 1972, when he said in effect that we absolutely need foreign investment. He added:
Since we don't have any alternative, at least in the short term, we can't have too restrictive a (national) policy on foreign investment.
This is an attitude that is quite prevalent among the less fortunate and less developed regions of the country. Officials of DREE were quoted by Dr. Springate in his paper.
In the presence of such an emotional issue, DREE has proceeded with this aim of attracting foreign investment to Canada. "We just keep a low profile in trying to attract multinational firms," said one official of the department who is active in investment promotion.
The premiers of the four Atlantic provinces have stated publicly that their provinces still require foreign investment if they are to make progress and reach the levels attained by the rest of Canada. Many of the witnesses appearing before the committee studying this bill made the same point.
But the point that stood out in my mind after reading the committee evidence and other articles is the fact that not only are many people in these various areas afraid that the government will legislate foreign capital out of the country but are also worried about this bill, because its implications are so- uncertain. The bill is so badly written that many people fear foreign investors will not even take initial steps to invest here because they do not know the ground rules that will be applied under the provisions of this bill. This is the danger that I see. This is the danger that my party has stressed. The regulations may be so uncertain, and give so much discretionary authority to the federal government that they will discourage foreign investment in those areas of the country where it is still needed, and yet there is nothing in the bill to encourage Canadians to move in and take up the slack.
This is why two amendments have been proposed by my colleague from Central Nova, because if the effort to regulate foreign control is to succeed without destroying our whole national industrial policy, there must be consultation, realistic consultation, true consultation between the federal government and the provinces. At this stage of the game when so many people agree that foreign capital is still essential to the development of the country, we should be careful not to do anything that will discourage such investment from coming in, unless we can guarantee that it will be replaced from other sources.
My hon. friends in the NDP say, "There is no need to worry if you drive out U.S. or other foreign capital. There is lots of money here in Canada to take up the slack." They point to the fact that there was an outflow of capital from Canada last year. They say it is a simple matter to replace what is cut off by using available Canadian funds. Many hon. members of this House realize it is not as simple as that. Traditionally Canadians do not invest in Canada unless they are given some encouragement. Certainly, the present government has done nothing to encourage Canadians to invest in their own country.
