I will agree with that, and the most sensible. Here is the minister who has been given the task of making DREE work, who has continually told us of the problems he has met in the interference and inconsistencies offered by other government programs, which destroy the efforts of DREE. He has talked about government interference in regional problems, and certainly he is one minister who recognizes the problems. Like my colleague, I should like to quote a remark made by the minister. When we talk about this business of Canadian capital, and say we do not need to worry about foreign capital because Canadian capital will replace it. At page 7637 of the Hansard report of that same speech, still speaking of the need for foreign capital in the Atlantic region, the minister said:
... the biggest failing, in terms of Canadian control of the Canadian economy, over the past 50 years or so has been the lack of initiative and entrepreneurship and the timidity of a great deal of Canadian capital.
He went on to talk about the fact that Canadians did not take the opportunity to invest in the Atlantic region, and so it was left to foreign capital to come in and develop the fishing, lumber and mining industries. In fact, practically all the development that took place in the four provinces was due to the initiative of foreign capital. The minister spoke of the pitfalls that occur when foreign capital gets control of the resources. He referred to several big fish plants that had closed and someone mentioned Devco and several other enterprises.
This happens, of course, but I would also point out to the House something that the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) referred to; that the record of the Canadian corporations is no better in this respect. Canadian corporations, too, have moved in and bought small locally owned plants and then, within two or three years when the operation was not viable, have moved out. I could name a dozen instances, Mr. Speaker, and my colleague the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) referred to a plant which was taken over a few years ago by a Canadian corporation and which now is just a warehouse. This happens all the time, so it is not just the foreign corporations that are at fault. It does not matter whether the money is international or Canadian, naturally the investors are going to make their decisions on an economic basis, and if they have to close the plant they do so. The argument that international corporations have no

heart and do not consider the interest of the regions is not valid; it applies regardless of the ownership of capital.
If one read that speech without realizing that the minister had made it, one would almost think he was attacking the principles of the bill. He mentioned all the things that should happen, and the fact that it is very important that there be meaningful co-operation between the provinces and the federal government as well as with the industry in the area, but he also admits that many of the problems are due to the fact that there has not been consultation and co-operation between the governments involved. Industries have been established or assisted when it has been obvious that they could not succeed. Had there been local consultation the grants would not have been recommended.
All through his speech the minister pointed out the dangers of attempting to restrict foreign capital unless something can be done to encourage Canadian capital to take up the slack. While our postulations are the same, Mr. Speaker, our conclusions are the opposite. The minister takes the position that these departments have been set up and, therefore, in some cases when foreign capital begins to investigate the possibility of establishing in an area they have to go to the federal government for some type of assistance. He says, therefore, that there are plenty of safeguards in his department to ensure provincial input and provincial co-operation. This is only partly true, Mr. Speaker. The type of consultation and co-operation that the minister mentions usually comes after many months of negotiation when the program is pretty well set up. At that time the company or the province usually comes to the federal government. That is not the type of meaningful co-operation that is needed if we are to establish viable ownership in these areas.
What we are talking about, and what the premiers of the provinces are talking about, is prior consultation and prior knowledge of what is going on. We have heard apologists for the bill on the government side say that this is provided in the bill. Mr. Speaker, there is nothing in the bill to establish prior consultation. The only stipulation in the bill, and it appears more than once, is that the minister "may" consult the provinces; after proceedings have gone so far he may hear provincial representations. How can representations be made on something about which you have no knowledge? If you do not know that there is an application, how can you make representations? This may be the government's definition of co-operation, and possibly that is why we have seen the confrontation between this government and Alberta or Quebec or various other provinces. We on this side do not consider it to be either consultation or co-operation.
In order to meet all the requirements of the foreign ownership program which the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion outlined so eloquently, there must be prior meaningful consultation and co-operation between the federal government and the provincial governments involved. That is why my colleague has introduced this amendment; that is why I say that this bill can be immeasurably strengthened by the government showing good faith. Let them show they really mean to follow a policy of consultation and co-operation by adopting these amendments and making the bill workable.
November 13, 1973

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps at this late hour, it would be worth while to pause in this debate and review historically why the ownership of our industry is in its present state. Let us hear what some of the people in the business community are saying about Bill C-132 and ask why this legislation is before this parliament at this time.
It is obvious to anyone remotely connected with business that a great deal of rationalization is afoot in certain nations and groups of nations. Many tariff walls are falling, a few are being raised. Considerable scientific research and industrial research is being carried out on a joint or on a multinational basis. Coupled with this, we have an alignment, or perhaps we should call it a realignment, of several European states into a common market with other smaller nations who are classed as associated states. Canada is not part of this alignment. In fact, it is a matter of embarrassment to this government that the European Economic Community has not responded in kind to the overtures made to it by this government.
The November 7 issue of the Montreal Gazette featured an editorial entitled "The Euro-Canadian Doldrums". It tells of the "brushoff" Canada has received from the European Economic Community. While Canada has appointed a senior ambassador to the EEC, that community has not established parallel representation in Ottawa. It is obvious to trading groups that specific spheres of influence in our industry are going to establish trade patterns that will last for many years. Many people in industry and many people throughout this country are asking where Canada fits into this picture. More pointedly, where does our industry fit into this picture?
From the turn of the century to 1973, all we have really done, in so far as industry ownership is concerned, is to have the largest percentage of ownership change from British to American. This is an historical fact. Bill C-132 will do little to change that course, but it is a first step, albeit a weak and faltering one, to attempt to change the thrust of the ownership of Canadian industry. Many people are concerned that we may be left out of industrial alignments or trading alignments and our trading position will be considered secondary to that of the United States. Their concern is justified, but this bill is not going to change that possibility.
There is a wave of nationalism in Canada at present. Much of it is well founded. We should have national aspirations and goals, but they should be realistic and attainable. We should be realistic enough in our outlook to be sure our national zeal does not move us into a position of isolation. If we move in that direction, then we will surely be left out of the market groups and trading blocs that are being formed.
It is proper at this point to note our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has been quick to accept invitations to visit Russia and China and had one scheduled for Chile until that country had some internal problems. However, we could not convince the Prime Minister to travel to Washington to talk trade with the Americans, or to Britain to discuss our falling trade balances with that country. He
Foreign Investment Review Act apparently cannot get an invitation to Europe to visit the EEC.
The thrust of Bill C-132 has caused much concern to segments of Canadian business. Let us hear what some of them have to say. The Calgary Chamber of Commerce says it is for the bill, with reservations, but points out that the bill deals with property and civil rights which are provincial matters. The Canadian Bankers Association is against the bill. They state that provisions of the Bank Act already limit foreign participation. I have yet to hear the Canadian Bankers Association or any Canadian bank come forward with a suggestion or recommendation to government as to what it could do to help develop Canadian business.
I have numerous letters from small and medium sized business complaining about the rates of interest charged by our banks. We have not heard from them how they will deal with government loans to small business, farmers and fishermen. They say they cannot make a profit at the rates set by government. But what about the large sums of money the government leaves on deposit in the various banks in Canada? Let the Canadian Bankers Association tell us the rate of interest they pay the government for the average of those deposits. Maybe we could play one off against the other.
The Canadian Bar Association sees problems with ministerial discretion, as do several others who submitted briefs. All agree it should be limited. They also see an infringement on the rights of Canadians to dispose of their business holdings as they see fit. The Canadian Chamber of Commerce is for the bill with reservations. Like many others who submitted briefs, they comment on the intrusion of government into the economic process of the private sector. They further contend that the bill is strongly biased against foreign investment and they state it creates a conflict between the provincial and federal governments.
The Canadian Chemical Producers Association are against the bill and state it is negative and discriminatory. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture is for the bill with reservations, but feels the bill is not specific enough regarding its effect on farm industry. The Canadian Manufacturers Association is against the bill saying, among other things, that it will have a detrimental effect on small business in Canada.
We received something like 50 or 60 submissions. The minister of finance of the province of Saskatchewan expressed his approval of the actions proposed in Bill C-132 in so far as they represent a step forward in dealing with problems of foreign ownership. He questioned the discretionary powers of the minister. In spite of the criteria set out in the legislation for making assessments, recommendations will still be arbitrary and judgemental. This is of concern to Saskatchewan.
George Wimpey Canada Limited, a large building and engineering contractor, is for the bill with some amendments. They say that the definition of "Canadian business" is general and would include land acquisitions which would result in classification as "non-eligible". That the concept of "unrelated business" requires clarification. That is the thrust of many of the briefs presented. The companies do not feel the language is clearcut.

Foreign Investment Review Act
W. Darcy McKeough said the province of Ontario is generally for the bill with reservations. He said this bill is only considered as a first step. More effective control of foreign investment should follow within a specified time period. A more detailed list of factors should be considered in the review process, including cultural criteria. The federal government should provide the province in which the foreign investment is proposed with a copy of the notification and any additional information submitted by the foreign investor. There were many submissions by business and provinces along this line. Mr. McKeough concluded by saying the bill should provide a statutory right of appeal to the courts in the case of any rulings or decisions under it, including the minister's rulings.
Richard Hatfield, the premier of New Brunswick, is against the bill. He feels it would be harmful to New Brunswick's attempts to attract and to accelerate industrial developments. National policy on foreign investments is of varying applicability to regions. It would adversely affect the Maritimes. For example, the New Brunswick Development Corporation helped launch 76 projects since 1970, for which half the total investment came from foreign sources. Previous speakers expanded on that view of Mr. Hatfield. It is very valid and we should listen to it.
Investment Dealers' Association of Canada are for the bill with reservations. They say there is a lack of provision for a formal summary procedure for determining whether a transaction is, in fact, an acquisition of control. The Mining Association of Canada is against the bill. They say that provincial and federal governments, with present legislation, have enough power to safeguard the ownership and control of Canada's mineral resources. Monarch Construction Limited, a firm similar to Wimpey, is against the bill but agrees with the principle. Their major objection is that having to submit bids on land to clearance by review agency would reduce Monarch's competitive position because of the delay factor.
Reichhold Chemicals Limited of Weston, Ontario, a 60 per cent Canadian held corporation, say there are more effective ways to control economic environment than by stifling foreign investment. In other words, they are saying what I said previously that we should encourage more investment in Canada by Canadians. Stelco, one of the largest Canadian corporations, is for the bill, with reservations. It says the regulations and prohibitions should be restricted to cases where there would be a clear injury to society, and should not unnecessarily interfere with freedom of action by individuals. It says the onus should be on the Crown to prove all aspects of its case, including whether the legislation applies to any particular person.
The Toronto Stock Exchange is for the bill, with reservations. It states that foreign portfolio investors who do not represent any threat to Canadian control are not able to ascertain quickly, in present circumstances, whether they are free to invest. Foreign investment should not be entirely discouraged. So the submissions go on. There are some 50 or 60 of them and a similar thread runs through them all. What Bill C-132 lacks, in my view, is supporting legislation or government policy to create and foster growth of small and medium sized businesses in Canada.

There has been some talk about the reorganization of the Industrial Development Bank, but what is required are amendments to the Bank Act and to the Income Tax Act which will create an atmosphere in which business can grow and develop and look outward beyond our shores into Europe and Asia. We need a government in office which will come to grips with our trading partners to the south and improve relations with them to the point at which we can attain the special status we have always enjoyed.
The success of Bill C-132 will not be determined by the bill itself. The measure before us is a weak, ineffective, faltering first step. But success will come if the appropriate supporting legislation is brought forth. It will come when the government realizes that regardless of the trade opportunities available to us in Russia and China, we shall always be tied to the United States in economic matters. I do not find this to be any great problem. I am aware that some of the people in the New Democratic Party are so anti-American they would build a Berlin wall on our borders; I know they cannot share my view. But most Canadian businessmen believe they can compete in the United States market on equal terms, and they say to us: Don't legislate us into a corner.
The success of the bill depends on whether or not the federal government is able to see the provincial point of view. As long as the provinces must go outside Canada to get loans at reasonable rates of interest, and as long as they must sell the bulk of their bonds and debentures outside the country, we shall not find a financial atmosphere in Canada which is conducive to the development and realization of industrial aspirations.

The success of this bill will depend upon how well the government handles inflation. One of the most perplexing difficulties facing industry at the present time is the increasing cost of some of the materials they use, coupled with shortgages of materials in certain sectors. The success of the bill will depend, too, upon whether or not the government can reach agreement with the provinces on tax-sharing arrangements. Each province has its development programs affecting industry and natural resources. We see the federal government trading off one part of the country against another, while at the same time talking about federalism. This is hardly the way to encourage agreement on industrial development.
Thus, as hon. members will appreciate, there are many factors outside this bill which will determine its successful operation, or the reverse. I am not convinced that hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches are capable of bringing forth the necessary supporting legislation to create the right atmosphere. It is a dismal picture when one contemplates the government's lack of direction in trade matters, particularly when they must depend upon the NDP for support. The NDP, with its well known anti-American stand, is hardly the party to encourage legislation which is broad, mature and outward-looking in temper and thrust.
Nevertheless, we will pass this bill along the third reading, with the reservations I have noted. I say again, as I have before, that if the government is not up to the task before it, it should, in the interest of Canada, step aside and let those who see the picture more clearly come to grips with the problem.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity to present my views on foreign investment specifically as it relates to areas which have been designated by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion as areas eligible for special government programs for the encouragement of industry, specifically manufacturing and processing operations. I wish, also, to
Foreign Investment Review Act explain why I believe the amendments presented by my colleagues are essential for the strengthening of Bill C-132.
I firmly believe that any legislation can be improved, and I suggest the amendments presented by my hon. friends are designed to do exactly this; in other words, to strengthen the legislation and make it more meaningful.
For the last decade at least, many Canadians, I would think especially those who are somewhat younger than the average age of members of this House of Commons, have been concerned with having a distinct Canadian nationality and with the very attributes of what Canadian nationalism should really be. A distinct facet of this search has been the question of, to what extent should we have foreign investment in this country and to what extent should we control foreign investment? By "foreign investment" I mean the type of foreign investment for which we are looking, be it from American, German, Japanese or other sources.
While the question of buying Canada back, or making Canada uniquely Canadian, whatever these cliches mean, has a lot of appeal today, not only to Canadians generally but especially to younger Canadians, in coming to grips with the matter I think it behooves all members to examine the central question, and in doing so not to go overboard on one side of the question, as members are so often in the habit of doing, and say that in order to create a unique Canadianism we are going to control foreign investment right down the line. In taking this approach, often we do not look to the end of the road and examine the damaging effects on the economy and on job creation in Canada. Therefore, we must have some form of balance between these two positions.
Since the days of confederation the CPR has been a prime example of foreign investment that has been used for the development of Canada. While this investment brought much benefit to Canada, it was often regarded by many people, especially those in western Canada, as a controlling factor in the development of the western Canadian economy rather than an encouragement to new growth. Although new growth was developed, it was always felt that the capital generated by that particular company often went out of the area in which it was most needed.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
In creating the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, the government recognized the fact that foreign or non-Canadian investment to create manufacturing and processing industries in regionally depressed areas can be of great benefit. During some questions which I asked the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) in the committee a while ago an exchange developed in regard to where the best record of DREE has b.een when the investment picture is looked at.
At that time I criticized the department for what I said was investing money in industries where very often I felt market research had been limited. Investments had been made in companies 40 miles away from where the same type of company had gone broke. I had examples of this in my own riding. The minister indicated that he felt that up

November 13, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act to the moment DREE's best success record had been where DREE had gotten together with established companies, be they Canadian or foreign-owned, which were willing to invest in regionally economically depressed areas jointly with DREE, and often with local investors, in order to create new industries. I think the track record of DREE is much better in the area of joint development with existing companies than it has been in cases where funds are provided to people who might just have had a dream at best.
While I personally accept the proposition that we want a truly Canadian identity, and with it investment on a controlled basis in Canada, those of us who come from regionally depressed areas are not anti foreign investment. We need that investment. But in saying that, we are also saying we would like to see incentives given, through a system of tax credits, to Canadians to invest in the expansion of Canadian industry within those regionally depressed areas.
We all know that the largest amount of foreign investment in Canada has gone into our resource industries. Nowhere are we more aware of this than in western Canada. It finds expression in the petroleum industry, in the gas industry and in the mining industry. We are all familiar with the fact that 99 per cent of the petroleum industry is foreign-owned.

speechtext: And look at the disaster we have had.

speechtext: They are living disasters.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
If a Canadian identity is to be developed, and if control of foreign investment is the way to do it, then I submit to the government that it should strengthen Bill C-132 in such a way that the aspirations of the regionally depressed areas are not thwarted as they attempt to engender investment that will create jobs and develop resource industries. I make that submission to the government in the hope that it will review once again its stance on consultation. Consultation can take place at any time, but consultation in a crisis situation, which comes about only after the crisis has developed and the premier of the province rears up and defies the federal government, is not the type of thing that we are looking for.
I find it very interesting that my NDP colleagues to my left feel that foreign investment can best be controlled by nationalization. They feel that this is the panacea. Nationalize everything, they say, and this will solve all our problems. Let me point out to those hon. friends to my left that the province of Manitoba has a socialist premier, even though some people question whether he is a socialist. When asked whether he was a socialist, he said, "Yes, I am a socialist, but firstly I am a pragmatist". His pragmatic approach to government led him to go to such foreign capitalist areas as New York City to find out whether or not capital could actually be obtained by the province of Manitoba for the development of the Manitoban economy, and I would say he was somewhat successful.
Let me also point out that the government of Manitoba has a tremendous record of failure in its Manitoba Development Corporation. I should like to give an example of 
this. That corporation helped to build the Lord Selkirk II, a ship plying Lake Winnipeg that has been used for many conferences held by the NDP government in Manitoba. It has a strange reputation, Mr. Speaker. It has the only bar in Manitoba which is losing money. So I question whether nationalization is really the panacea it is said to be.
Seriously, what bothers me most about the NDP approach is that they seem to be willing to expand our energy resources to buy back Canada, whatever that means. Rather, let us use the investment capital that we can generate as Canadians to develop new industries. Let us use that capital to develop our resource industries.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: You just do not like our methods, that is all.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: No, I do not. I submit to the government that we should use this Canadian money to develop our resources in order to provide more labour-intensive industrial areas.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: That's a socialist approach.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: I do not think it is a socialist approach. It is a common sense approach, without nationalization. It is rather interesting to hear that the NDP somewhat agrees with one plank in an economic policy that has already come full circle. I point out that fundamentally this is nationalism, and I am in no way a proponent of this policy because I have seen its failure in areas even within Manitoba.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: We are just glad to know that Manitoba people always agree.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak specifically about the amendments proposed, and clearly give my views to the government as to why they are essential to the strengthening of Bill C-132. As I have already pointed out, there are certain merits to this bill and there is a desire to have some control over foreign investment. This desire is not unique in Canada. Every western industrialized nation has some form of control over foreign investment. This is nothing out of the ordinary. But what we must keep in mind is that Canada is a federalist state having ten provinces and a central government, and in no way in respect of future economic development should the central government unilaterally declare this is the way things are to be done, because this affects the provincial governments and the economic lifeblood of each.
It is staggering to the imagination that the federal government would be willing to pass a bill in which it has the option to consult. At some future time the government may say it intends to consult with a province, but there might be an industry which is willing to come to Manitoba to invest, thus creating jobs, and it would be up to the federal government to decide whether that would be good for Manitoba. Surely the Manitoba government, representing the people of that province, should have some voice as to whether such an industry should locate there.
This matter of consultation has become abundantly clear to us. Within recent days, with the energy crisis, the federal government, in what I would call a very naked
November 13, 1973

political approach to the problem, has come out with a policy-supposedly to be changed whenever it is politically expedient-which, in its hope, will ease this crisis. Producing provinces have always had the right to a return on the resources which exist in the province. The federal government now simply goes ahead without consultation, and in fact with confrontation, and says it is going to establish an energy policy without even asking the provinces whether they agree. Surely the least the government could do when it comes to foreign investment is to avoid this type of confrontation.
It is the very nature of a federalist system to consult. This is not a legislative union, this is a federalist state. I submit that Bill C-132, without the amendments proposed by my colleagues, is a bill which is much weaker and will lead to very serious confrontation between the provinces and the federal government if this government is willing to exercise the jurisdiction it will receive through passage of the bill.
I would like to see foreign and Canadian investment encouraged in Canada. Western Canada needs foreign investment, we need better tax credit programs and incentives which will encourage confidence on the part of holders of small portfolios to invest in Canadian industry. This is essential.
A Science Council study pointed out that Canada has one of the lowest percentages of workers employed in the manufacturing sector of any industrialized country. If we are to approach anywhere near full employment, let us not say that foreign investment is to be discouraged. We should not cut it back, because certain areas in Canada require foreign investment while in other areas perhaps it has gone far enough. In this area we must take into account growth factors, how far growth should be allowed and how fast it should be allowed. But because of regional differences, our growth factors are not similar or parallel. Some of our areas need the foreign investment which I am afraid Bill C-132 would thwart.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in summarizing some of the thoughts I expressed prior to the six o'clock recess, I should like to refer to three points. The first is that nationalization of industries is not the manner by which Canadian content or the amount of Canadian investment in industries in Canada should be increased. The answer is not suggested so often by members of the New Democratic Party. I categorically reject it.
Second, whatever foreign review we might engage in so far as foreign investment is concerned, let us not make the review in such a manner that it becomes a disincentive for foreign investment, especially in depressed areas and areas of regional economic disparity where foreign investment is desperately needed. Third, as Canadian leaders we should encourage Canadian investment in Canadian
Foreign Investment Review Act industry, especially in manufacturing and secondary processing, in order that a balance might again be established between foreign investment and Canadian ownership.
I feel one method by which we could obtain this balance would be by offering incentives through which we could encourage employee participation in the ownership of companies. A number of industrialized countries have been successful in this type of approach. Second, we should make incentives available, especially for small businesses. We should encourage greater investment in such businesses so that jobs are created. Tax credits should be granted so that more people would be willing to invest risk capital, especially in smaller Canadian businesses.
In many areas of western Canada, to a great degree jobs are created by small industries. If we could provide benefits through tax incentives for companies to invest in Canada, not only would we have a broader balance but we would create the jobs which are desperately needed. A change should be brought about in succession duties so that when death occurs the beneficiaries of a small business are not forced to sell out very often to a foreign-financed company because of the ready availability of cash. Rather, some kind of tax credit should be provided whereby succession duties will not be so prohibitive as to force beneficiaries to sell Canadian companies.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all persons seeking public office have reason for so doing. The lack of effective action by the present government in protecting and developing Canadian control of our economic destiny was one of the three prime concerns which motivated my quest for this office.
During the years from 1968 to 1972 there were three takeover attempts which the government was called upon to deal with in the energy field. Each was a matter of "significant benefit" to Canada. Each was dealt with separately. Dennison Mines was refused permission to sell. Home Oil was placed in a situation of remaining Canadian. However, the third, Supertest Petroleum, was allowed to fall under foreign ownership and control.
I have no argument with the first two decisions. The third, however, is of great concern because the outlets of Supertest are spread throughout my section of Canada. It was the slogan of Supertest that it was an "all-Canadian company". Indeed, these words still remain on some gas stations though the company is clearly no longer allCanadian. Clearly, it could have remained so since it was a profitable Canadian-owned company, and a home with a Canadian- owned firm could surely have been found if there had been concern by the government that this be done.
It is true that the terms of this bill set up a system other than that which existed under the government's arbitrary decision-making, but clearly the government's will will continue to play a part in decision-making since law is always open to varied interpretations. I suggest it was public pressure that saved Home Oil, not government direction. I suggest it was lack of public pressure that saw Supertest slip away.
Under this bill there is no definite, positive direction; there is merely a more formalized screening that would

November 13, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act
not necessarily save those Canadian companies that remain from being absorbed. This is an indictment of the government, an indictment which proves that it still has no firm commitment to anything that will in substance assist us in controlling our own destiny but, rather, a commitment to pass into law a bill which can be used as window-dressing in an effort to convince Canadian voters that action is being taken.
Style, not substance, has been the technique of this government in its five years of life-style in holding conferences and ignoring the promises made, style in appointing commissions and never forcing them to report, style in hurriedly implementing programs and then having moneys wasted on jerry-built schemes. The Canadian people need more than style, they want more than style, and they deserve more than style.
Perhaps the most unfortunate aspect of the bill is that when it becomes law people will perceive that something has been done, when in fact it has not, and the pressure for real and meaningful steps to be taken will abate for a time. The pressure will abate and this will make the job all the more difficult in the future. That there is a real concern by Canadians, and a real need to develop and implement positive programs, cannot be doubted.
Fifteen years of dealing daily with the youth of our country-as a student at university and as a teacher of history in the high schools of Ontario-has convinced me that there is an ever-growing concern in this respect. This concern has not been allayed during these years, nor will it be allayed by this bill.
There is, in fact, a real danger that the polarization represented by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on the one hand and the New Democratic Party on the other will leave those of us who believe in positive, responsible government action at a disadvantage. The Prime Minister time and time again has compared government action in Canada to the Cuban revolution. He has held up the spectre of radically decreased living standards if steps are taken to control the effects of foreign investment. He gives only two alternatives: do nothing, or suffer greatly. We have done nothing, and we have suffered greatly in any case through unemployment and inflation running unabated at high levels.
If my information coming from the Niagara peninsula is correct, the shortages which are occurring in Bell Canada cable, in hydro cable, in insulation, brick and aluminum siding, will bring the construction industry to a halt. We are short of even such things as tires and anti-freeze at the distribution level. If such shortages, some of which apparently have lasted since last June, are not corrected we will suffer greatly again, not because of lack of effective control of foreign investment but because of general economic mismanagement. The Prime Minister's gross distortion of the choices that face Canada, and his inaction, have spurred the NDP to hold out the need for state intervention on a massive scale as the only means and as the dogmatic truth.
Our youth are responsible citizens, and they are desirous of seeing Canada controlled by Canadians. But because the loud trumpet notes carry farthest, the respon-

sible middle ground is often lost to their ears. In years gone by I have attempted to seek the opinion of the youth in my area. I have participated in the deliberations of the Young Progressive Conservative Association of Ontario as it surveyed the opinion of our youth in the wider area. The conclusions reached by these soundings have been that the young people want the government to provide leadership, that they are willing to accept sacrifice and to play whatever role they can in bringing about the desired result.
The onus that falls upor. us as members of parliament is to provide constructive leadership. The present government has not done this. The NDP is blatantly emotional and anti-American in its mouthings, and thus cannot be constructive. Therefore, the burden must fall upon the Conservative Party to provide the constructive Canadian-ism that our youth seek and that our country so badly needs. I will have more to say about this later.
Is there a need for expanded Canadian ownership and control and for positive measures to assist in bringing these about? In my experience, there is no doubt at all that there is. Last week, acquaintances of mine from Denmark arrived in Canada after a week's visit in the United States. They came to look for products that could be purchased in Canada and merchandised in Denmark and, through their connections, in six other countries in Europe both within and without the European Common Market.
To their satisfaction-and these are men with buying experience in all parts of the world-certain of our products were of a higher quality than those produced in the United States and were capable of competing successfully in European markets. When they asked about these Canadian-produced goods, when they talked about exporting, they were told there would have to be consultation with home offices to see if these Canadian firms could export. How will this bill remedy such a situation? Surely it cannot and will not-and Canadian jobs based on export will not develop.
In Niagara Falls, as well, orders went to U.S. plants when work was slack in a Canadian company because of management decisions, even though the Canadian plant was more efficient. This firm has since changed ownership and aggressive Canadian control has led to expansion of the work force and of the plant. There is also a foreign-owned but Canadian-operated firm which could be Canadian-owned if money were available for the management to buy it out. It has the potential to penetrate the U.S. market if it could obtain capital to expand the production of its excellent product.
Case after case can be cited where Canadian interests are not best served, and this bill does nothing to correct that situation. Case after case can be cited where Canadian-owned or operated firms are unable to expand because capital sources are not available to them on terms they are capable of handling. It is certain that unless positive steps are taken, this bill will solve none of the problems I have mentioned and in fact may cause harm by preventing expansion unless other capital sources are available. Also, it may create a false sense of security which can lead to our economy coming even more under foreign domination.
At this point may I state that it is control, more than ownership, that concerns me. Ownership implies a reasonable return for investment. This is right and just for
November 13, 1973

anyone who believes in capitalism, in someone other than the state undertaking business enterprises. It is the direction that a business takes that is the real concern. If it is, as in some cases, a direction that maximizes output for sale in Canada and abroad-with attendant increases in Canadian labour and resource input-then it is a fair bargain. If it is a direction which seeks raw materials from Canada and components from other Canadian-based operations, then it is a fair bargain. But if it is a direction restricting competition to the Canadian market, regardless of ability to compete, and if it is a direction maximizing the use of foreign-produced goods, then it is not a fair bargain and action must be taken. The bill before us provides no steps in this direction.
Is the state the only mechanism through which we can regain Canadian control? Must there be massive state intervention and nationalization before something can be done? Is outright socialism the only way? Personally, I believe there is a better way. But no other way has been tried, so the socialists can point to continuing failure and beat their drums of nationalization. Perhaps the socialists are right. Perhaps Canadians are not capable of reaching out to control their own destiny with government assistance. But this is questionable, because Canadians have never been asked or given the opportunity by this government to share in obtaining this control. It may be that Canadians are not willing or capable of doing so. It may be that only the government can change the direction in which we are proceeding. But I do not believe so and I will bend every effort to see that Canadians are given a chance to participate before the heavy and inefficient hand of state ownership comes to this country.
Lest our socialist friends jump to the conclusion that I am a classical Liberal calling for no action by the state, or a complete "free enterpriser" unwilling to see the government intervene in the economy, may I make these points of clarification. The first duty of a government, in my view, is to assess the needs of its people; the second is to set objectives to satisfy these needs; the third is to assist and encourage private citizens in their striving to reach these objectives.
Clearly, the need of the Canadian people is to control their own destiny. The objective is to make this country as productive as possible and to provide all of us with a good and continually improving life. The means, just as clearly, must be to have the government provide whatever assistance is needed for Canadians to increase their productivity and to control our economy if it is agreed that Canadians will work more for themselves than will foreigners. The role of the state is not to provide for the well-being of individuals, but to produce circumstances whereby they can best provide for themselves-where through their energy and initiative a better life can be developed.
The government of the day has not set down clearly defined objectives. Indeed, through its various ministers it has tried at one time or another to grasp all sides of the spectrum. The government has not provided the means whereby individuals can, acting alone or together with state agencies, participate in maintaining or regaining control of our economic destiny on any regular basis. The positive steps that have been taken, such as interest being written off, have come only after provincial initiative has
Foreign Investment Review Act made it necessary to act. True, the CDC has been established with the promise of participation, but without the substance of involvement. Indeed, the use of tax laws to provide incentive has been suggested, but not adopted as yet. The designating of key sector in the economy has been suggested, but not followed up. The provision of low interest capital equal to foreign loans has been suggested, but not acted upon.
Surely these and other alternatives could be brought into effect by a government concerned about setting positive directions and assisting with positive programs. We are a people who, through our history, have had confidence in our government, as witnessed by lack of civil strife compared with other states. We are a people who have been provided with leadership and assistance from governments in the past. Today we are a people who will respond to constructive Canadianism. I wonder how much further we would be on the path of grasping firmly the reigns of our own destiny if some of the positive programs put forward by the PC party had been implemented years ago?
Opportunities for Youth and LIP grants do not provide permanent jobs. If the money spent on these programs had been put into capital assistance, jobs would have been provided. The advertising moneys spent on telling our senior citizens that they would get $2.88 more, displaying flower-pots and saying, "It is up to us," and encouraging us to use a zip code have long gone, with no real lasting effect although they totalled hundreds of thousands of dollars. How much greater and longer lasting would have been the results of these advertising campaigns if they had been aimed at encouraging Canadians to participate in an effective Canadian Development Corporation, or advertised the fact that Canadian entrepreneurs would be assisted in their efforts to share in directing Canada's economy for the benefit of Canadians?
Instead today we are faced with the reality of a bill that will do little but which I am certain, come the next election, will be called a great leap forward by every Liberal candidate in the land. Fortunately, the Canadian people have had enough of style and subterfuge and will recognize the substance of the Conservative policies and the opportunities that these will present to them when implemented. Among them will be a policy of encouraging the incentive that exists in our people, marshalling our resources to the task of obtaining as much independence as possible in economic decision-making.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with much attention to a number of hon. members who have spoken on these amendments. I am surprised at the lack of sympathy for the federal system shown by some of my colleagues and their lack of appreciation of the obligations which must be met by the federal government in designing a program covering foreign investment and implementing it in the national interest.
I have heard much comment from some of my colleagues in the House on the amount of influence they feel the provinces should have in deciding the degree of permissible foreign control. I am in complete disagreement with those who believe that the provinces should decide, sepa-

Foreign Investment Review Act rately in their own interests, what should be the interest and obligation of the federal government. Later on I intend to move an amending motion that I am sure will add to the position taken by some of my colleagues in this House. If they want all the provinces to make this decision simply because they have friends in certain provinces, it seems to me to be a grave oversight to omit the executive councils of the territories that are not yet provinces but which possess great potential in terms of natural resources.
I have always believed that a Canadian in one part of Canada should be equal to a Canadian in another part of Canada. For a long time I have lived in northern Ontario, an area rich in resources but where this has not been a fact. This is an area which has supported southern Ontario, in particular Toronto and Montreal, and the financial institutions of the country. It did so initially at a time when other parts of the country were producing very little to contribute to national income and national productivity. And in that area we have never received our fair share from either the federal government or the provincial government.
I suggest that some hon. members of this House should look at some of the disadvantaged areas of Canada. They should look at the Maritimes which have contributed a great deal of industrial input to Canadian society over the years. The Maritimes have provided the resource base for other sectors of Canada. Some of that contribution came to my area because maritimers also came there to help develop our resources.
The people of Great Britain did not bring about the industrial revolution there all on their own. Certainly initiative was shown in the invention of the cotton-jenny and in developments in the mining industry at the beginning of the industrial age. But one of the main contributions came in the form of capital supplied from Switzerland, by the people of Germany, by Dutch people, as well as by some of the landed gentry in Britain. That sparked the industrial revolution and produced a great nation that eventually was able to establish the Commonwealth of Nations which in turn has really been responsible for the development of half the world as we know it today.
Years later, when the industrial revolution began in the United States, again capital was needed. This has always been the case and always will be the case. Capital came from countries such as Switzerland, Holland and Great Britain, but it was supplied to the United States in the form of loans. It took 100 years to develop the industrial revolution in England. It took probably 30 to 40 years to do the same in the United States. Both were financed with imported capital, but in both cases that imported capital represented borrowings by the particular country or by the particular industries in that country.
In Canada, our industrial revolution was late in starting. We are one of the richest natural resource countries in the world, and our development was begun by the use of our pioneering spirit in conjunction with the use of outside capital. But the difference between our industrial revolution and those of Great Britain and the United States is that in Canada we sold our resources to other countries. We sold our resources to the people who had the

capital. The people who came in did not lend Canadians capital; instead, they bought the resources.
At present, a great controversy is taking place in my area. In it we have probably the highest hill in Ontario. It is about 1700 feet high. In effect, it is a resource that cannot be duplicated anywhere else in Ontario. At present, the provincial Conservative government is talking about spending $82 million in my area. I certainly have no objection to that if it will do anything for the people of Timiskaming.
What are we talking about really, Mr. Speaker? We are again talking about selling our resources-selling a piece of land to Holiday Inns and a number of other American companies. Tourists will come to the area for $100 a day or $200 a day and take advantage of whatever resources are there. We will have bellboys and waiters, but certainly we will not have cooks because for $100 a day they will want cooks from Paris. But we will have sold our resources, and $20 million or $30 million of that amount will have come from the people of Ontario.
It would seem to me, Mr. Speaker, that it is time we made a decision. We are God-blessed with resources, but we are certainly not God-blessed with the ability to develop them. We sell everything that is not nailed down, and we are willing to sell some things that are nailed down as well. I have heard some of my colleagues in the Conservative Party speak today about the desire of the provinces to have an input. Provinces be damned!

In my opinion we have developed an attitude in this country that is not to our advantage. We hear about separatism in Quebec. We may talk about separatism because of linguistic differences or because a province is willing to give away its resources, but it is all the same. I think my colleagues in the Conservative Party had better look at some of the resources that they are going to defend on behalf of the provincial governments. One of the Conservative governments owns most of the oil potential in Canada at the present time, and I live in a province with a Conservative government that needs the major portion of that oil.

I will not know that until I know how much electricity and oil I am going to get this winter. That is true of all Canadians. One of our major problems is the oil industry, which is 99 per cent foreign-controlled. I think it is a disgrace to allow one of our major resources to be controlled 99 per cent by American interests. We have been willing to sell these resources, Mr. Speaker. I do not suggest that we buy them back, but I do suggest that they
November 13, 1973

are still Canadian resources which belong to the Canadian people. Every member of parliament is going to find it very difficult to persuade a constituent who complains that he does not have enough oil for his furnace that it is all right for most of it to go south of the border. I suggest that it is time we controlled our economy and our destiny.
I was shocked to learn recently that our troops were not acceptable as members of the peacekeeping force in the Middle East. It turned out that we were acceptable in the end because, as a member of the NATO forces, we were balanced by Poland as a member of the Warsaw Pact. If we are to maintain our reputation in matters like peacekeeping, it seems to me we must establish control at home. We are no poorer than countries such as Mexico and others which have decided it may be necessary to tighten the belt. It may be necessary to establish our Canadian independence and our ability to play a role as an independent nation industrially, commercially, philosophically, and politically if necessary.
If my colleagues believe that the provinces have a role, I am not sure what it should be, but they should have some input into the question of federal control of the Canadian economy. The provinces should not have a veto. If my colleagues in the Conservative Party believe in the veto, then it should also be extended to the territories of Canada which have uncontrolled resources. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett):
That motion numbered 2 be amended by inserting in line 7 thereof, following the words "a province" the words, "or a territorial council".
I move this motion, Mr. Speaker, because I believe that what is fair to the ten provinces is also fair for the territories which have not yet been raped but obviously will be raped if we do not provide a national philosophy that will give full play to the development of Canada rather than to the development of veto power.
This is an important bill, but it is a lousy bill. The Liberal Party never had a philosophy that would take them far enough toward solving a problem. This bill is part of a solution. If anybody asks why we did not support the Conservative Party and so call an election right away, it was the fear that the Conservatives would form the government of Canada.

I believe that most of the amendments introduced by the Conservative Party are divisive. I understand the Liberal Party will be supported by the Conservatives on this bill. Therefore, I suggest that they do something about the bill, strengthen it as much as possible, so that we can develop a strong, independent nation. In that way we will no longer be the nominee of the United Nations for a peacekeeping force. Canadians are independent enough in industrial development, resource development and international relations to be looked upon by the rest of the world not as an industrial satellite of the United States but as people willing to spend money to develop our resources and make whatever sacrifices are necessary.
I move this amendment in the hope that my proposal for unity will be accepted by the Liberals and Conservatives so that those people in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon will be able to play an equal role with the provinces in dividing the spoils of Canada.
