speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House of Commons is studying Bill C-132, entitled an Act to provide for the review and assessment of acquisitions of control of Canadian business enterprises by certain persons and of the establishment of new businesses in Canada by certain persons.
Since the beginning of this debate, Mr. Speaker, Progressive Conservatives and New Democrats have proposed a number of amendments which I have read without seeing how they can really change the spirit of this bill. Generally speaking, they seem to simply play around in this bill which, itself, solves nothing much. This may be a harsh judgment, but let me read the very beginning of this bill.
2. (1) This Act is enacted by the Parliament of Canada in recognition by Parliament that the extent to which control of Canadian industry, trade and commerce has become acquired by

November 13, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act
persons other than Canadians and the effect thereof on the ability of Canadians to maintain effective control over their economic environment is a matter of national concern, and that it is therefore expedient to establish a means by which measures may be taken under the authority of Parliament to ensure that, in so far as is practicable after the enactment of this Act...
Mr. Speaker, if you read the preambule of this legislation you find that as far as possible the government will try to implement Bill C-132 to achieve a certain degree of control over foreign corporations or foreign investment in Canada.
But such a control can be implemented financially only. I remember a report that was tabled in the House, a report which had been prepared for the Privy Council Office and was entitled "Foreign Ownership and the Structure of Canadian industry", Report of the Task Force on the Structure of Canadian Industry.
A Crown minister was the sponsor of this study and under the responsibility of the then President of the Privy Council this task force carried out this study and took rather radical positions requesting the government to take energetic measures. Of course, the government did not agree with the conclusions of this study. Later on, further studies were prepared with a view to demonstrating to parliamentarians and Canadians in general that Canada did not belong to us anymore or only a very small part of it.
I will quote only one excerpt from this study. It is taken from page 87 and I quote:
35. An alternative means of Canadian participation in the profits of direct investment firms is minority Canadian ownership. The extent of such participation by Canadians is at present relatively limited, reflecting the strong preference of foreign corporations for operating abroad through wholly-owned subsidiaries.
Those are statistics which rebut anything the minister responsible for this legislation told us as well as the spokesmen for the Progressive Conservative and the NDP parties.
For 375 of the largest non-financial Canadian corporate complexes in Canada (for a detailed discussion of these and other data on this topic,...), 162 or 43 per cent are private companies with no publicly traded shares, and about 75 per cent of these private companies are controlled by non-residents. It has been estimated that approximately 18 per cent of the total corporate taxable income in Canada in 1965 was earned by about 130 of the largest private corporations, most of which were foreign-owned.
Mr. Speaker, that is one problem. The second is the approach to or the participation of Canadian provinces in the protection of our economy and the ensurance of a steady development of our economy in the interest of, by and for all Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, one finds that once more such is not the case. At federal-provincial meetings, we witness lengthy discussions that end up in smoke or lead to practically nothing or big statements of intent. But in the end, Mr. Speaker, what tools are available to the provinces to really protect their own regional or local economy in the Canadian or North American context so the Canadian entity will be preserved? I must say, Mr. Speaker, that those means are more means in principle than effective financial means.

How did foreigners chiefly acquire control over our economy? With money. And what will be the way for all Canadians to regain the economy of their country? Again, with money.
Mr. Speaker, with respect to the James Bay development project, or the need for nuclear, electrical or petrochemical energy in Quebec and other provinces, what means are available to the provinces or to the federal government to provide for the protection of the Canadian control over such projects or such new essential and vital developments?
What do our governments do, whether they are Progressive Conservative or Liberal, provincial or federal? Once they have prepared a plan, once they have given it sufficient publicity to sell the idea to the public and do some window-dressing, then, Mr. Speaker, the little procession begins: the Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister, officials, the Minister of Natural Ressources, the Minister of Energy, the ambassador and all the others are going where? They are not asking the Canadian people to get in, in order to develop the country. They go abroad. They go to the United States, to other countries. On the pretence that they will create employment-poppycock again on the part of this government-they go to France where they try to convince the Michelin or Renault companies to settle in Canada to create employment in this country. Those firms are granted subsidies and the first thing we know, Mr. Speaker, is that it does not work, for all kinds of reasons.
I do not wish to weigh the situation to know whether they should be granted a subsidy or not, but I want to say that every time there is a desire to create employment, economic or financial, gigantic or fantastic projects, like James Bay, Hydro-Quebec or Ontario-Hydro projects or any other similar venture, they go begging, they negotiate with American people or foreigners, but especially with Americans. Then, they invite and help them invest in our own country. In return, the Prime Minister, the minister, or the government representative, whether on the federal or provincial level, may come forward, under the cover of a press conference with cocktails and all, rise and state in the faces of Canadians or Quebecers: "I am happy to announce that foreigners trust in the future of Quebec, in the future of Canada, and that thanks to that trust, we shall be able, from such or such date, to proceed with the development of the James Bay project or some other project".
Well, Mr. Speaker, that is a shame. I have nothing against foreigners eager to come and invest in our country; I suggest however that if foreigners trust in our future and see in our province or country a potential for economic development, if they have found resources worthy of being developed in a profitable way for Canadians, if they trust in the economy of Canada, why is it then that Canadians, and Quebecers in particular, should not have also the opportunity and the same trust to invest in our own country?
Mr. Speaker, I will give you just one concrete example on this subject. We know that under the new tax system implemented by this government, the savings of Canadians are taxable. The worker, the farmer or the day labourer cannot invest several hundred thousand dollars but
November 13, 1973

they could invest in Canadian businesses not only their work, the fruits of their labour but also their small savings. Even if he is poor, if he has plenty of guts the average citizen could invest but he cannot because the tax legislation discourages his willingness to save money. To invest he has to save money first.
Mr. Speaker, when the time comes to complete his income tax return, the average citizen receives from his bank a note telling him he has to pay taxes on his savings. Mr. Speaker, this system is all wrong. Then the government will tell us, referring to political principles in order to obtain votes, that it defends an economic nationalism policy and that it presented a bill that is honest and well-intentioned; it will tell us that it wants to give back Canada to Canadians through Bill C-132 or any other inquiry or brief.
Mr. Speaker, how far will Bill C-132 go? It will create another gizmo of civil servants which will be called the Foreign Investment Review Agency and will provide for the appointment of a commissioner. This bill also states, Mr. Speaker, that we shall pay the expenses of the large corporation representatives that we shall call before us.
Mr. Speaker, this indicates the intention of the government. Even if I read it in the newspapers or even if they repeated here ten or twenty times that this government is well intentioned in wishing to control Canadian business instead of nationalizing it as the New Democratic Party would want it, or to "play" with their profit as the Conservatives would want, I would not believe it. But if the government were well intentioned, Mr. Speaker, it would begin by allowing the provinces the financial possibility of ensuring the development of their own resources through financial means belonging to Canadians and Quebecers, that is the use of the Bank of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, if the Canadian government and the provinces trust American funds invested in our country and guaranteed by our values, I do not see why this same government, if it is really Canadian, if it is really elected to serve the interests of Canadians, would not use the Bank of Canada to invest in our own resources, since it is the same mortgage. Mr. Speaker, the government could then prove that it believes in Canada and I have no doubt that Canadians would follow its example.
I do not want to hear that Canadians do not control anything or that they are not interested in their country when their own government never gives them a good example and when it is crawling in front of foreign businesses, in front of foreign capital to develop our country.
Mr. Speaker, it is easy to preach in favour of Canadian unity. The other day, I heard a rather interesting remark. The Conservatives in western Canada say that the Liberal Party is a French-Canadian party and consequently that it is not a good party. Therefore they invite these people to vote Conservative.
At the same time, Liberals in eastern Canada say to the people that the Progressive Conservative party is an English-speaking party and, therefore, they should vote Liberal, for it is not a "representative" party.
Foreign Investment Review Act
Finally, both these so-called great national parties attempt to build up their political prestige, for this is what counts in the end, in order to prevent the division of the country.
However, the price for national unity is to be paid financially. We have here a Minister of Finance, as in each provincial legislature. If these people are honest and not puppets of high finance, but are there to serve the interests of the Canadian people, for which they have been elected, they will stop to think instead of flippantly rejecting solutions enabling the government and the Canadian people to regain control over the economy.
Mr. Speaker, I believe-and I think that the other hon. members of my party agree-in private enterprise and in individual initiative.
We are against economic nationalism whereby we must nationalize to be at home. We feel, Mr. Speaker, that in the system of free enterprise, the human being finds his strength, his vigour and his wish to better himself. We firmly believe that if a person is to live decently in free enterprise, earn his living and support his family, he must have the ambition to better himself.
It is the same for a country. If we want the provinces to wish to improve themselves and to grow together in this confederation, the federal government, which is here to harmonize relations, must provide them with the financial means necessary for their development, for instance by creating subsidiaries of the Bank of Canada in each province^
Mr. Speaker, this solution is rediculed, but it remains that the abject position of our Prime Minister when dealing with foreigners to develop James Bay is much sadder.
Mr. Speaker, I would have something else to say about that. Even if we believe in private enterprise, it does not mean that we are idiots. It is essential that private enterprise be supported. This government, through its own measures, had made private entreprise practically dependent on a new kind of social welfare.
We have been left with the impression that the government is responsible for the creation of employment, but this is an entirely wrong concept. The government alone could not create a single job. It was private enterprise that created those jobs in this country.
A problem that this bill tries to deal with is the control over investments in this country so that companies should be Canadian. But what steps can the government take in this regard? All it thought about was to create an agency.
Mr. Speaker, when I said at the outset of my comments that unless it is materially possible to have statistics available and to know who controls such and such company, we shall awaken in five or ten years with another so-called Gordon or Watkins report or another Bill C-132 and we will be no better for it. On the contrary, foreign capital will have continued to pour into our country.
If Canada is to develop, Mr. Speaker, it is not a question of doing what some members would like, that is send foreigners back to their country. There is so much room in Canada to develop and live. Those people have a right to live in our country. But, Mr. Speaker, if the government

November 13, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act really is Canadian, if it is not paid by foreigners, let it make use of the present financial means to develop our country without going to war against foreigners.
Mr. Speaker, this is exactly the same thing as when we say that English-speaking people are to blame when separatism is mentioned and when things are going bad in Quebec. In the Social Credit party, we say that the English-speaking people are not to blame, but that Quebecers are because they never gave themselves real representatives to lead them.
Let us stop saying that the English or the foreigners are to blame if we do not live suitably in Canada. It is our fault if we fail to give ourselves a truly Canadian government and if we keep on having governments paid, elected and controlled by high finance.
Would this government, which was elected by finance, be able through a bill to control its investments? This is totally ridiculous, Mr. Speaker. They are bluffing in an attempt to silence the nationalists who believe in Canada and, at the same time, leaders keep on currying favours with large companies. What is the difference between Progressive Conservatives and Liberals? Absolutely none: both are courting the same corporations and the same corporations contribute to replenish the electoral funds of these two parties. They in turns come into power without changing the situation at all.
Mr. Speaker, the NDP claims that the only way to solve the problem is to nationalize companies so as to make them companies of the state in order to see what is going to happen. They still believe in the CBC and in all these gimmicks. As for us, though small in number, we are sincere and we are Canadians. We believe in free enterprise, in the value of the person and his right to develop in free enterprise.
We are Canadians and we say that neither the English, nor the French Canadians nor the Americans are to be held responsible because Canada does not belong to Canadians any more; those responsible are the political maneuverers who get elected through finance, stay there with a title and serve financiers. As long as we have to bear with such politicians, the House waste its time on tame bills and Canada will still be sold to foreigners for a mess of pottage.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak to the subamendment offered by the hon. member for Timiskam-ing (Mr. Peters) with regard to motion No. 2 which is before us. When motion No. 2 in its original form was first debated, I made it clear that I thought the amendment would do nothing to strengthen the bill and that in fact it would have the effect of weakening the bill.
I should like briefly to review two points. The first is that as the bill now stands, it provides for the government to take into account provincial industrial and economic policies in respect of any province likely to be significantly affected. The amendment standing on the order paper, not the subamendment, focuses only on provinces in which the enterprise or the business is carried on or proposed to be carried on. The subamendment offered this evening is limited in exactly the same way. It would limit consideration with regard to provinces or territories only

to those provinces or territories in which the enterprise is carried on or in which the new business is proposed to be carried on.
Clearly, this would have the effect of narrowing the intent of the bill. It would have the effect of making it more inflexible than would the present wording. It would exclude, as I have mentioned already, provinces which were significantly affected. It would include only those provinces in which the enterprise is carried on or in which the proposed enterprise is to be carried on. Provinces significantly affected by the enterprise would be excluded from any consideration. That is the first point.
I should like to give an example of how this might work. For instance, it is quite conceivable that a province might be affected in a very substantial way by the existence of a new investment to be made or a new firm to be acquired in a province. One might visualize-I believe I used this example before-the case of a major tire manufacturing operation. A tire manufacturing operation which might be located, let us say, in Quebec could affect a major tire factory operating in the Maritimes. This could have an effect not only on the neighbouring province or provinces, but the new or proposed investment could equally have an effect upon existing tire manufacturing firms in other provinces including, for example, Ontario.
The subamendment offered to the original amendment would exclude any consideration of those provinces which would be significantly affected, because it limits the consideration to the province in which the enterprise, takeover or proposed investment would be carried on. A province may have a very large interest in a takeover or investment because of its position as a consuming province, or because of plants in that province that would be in a competitive position with the firm to be taken over or established.
I submit that the first amendment, No. 2, would weaken the bill because it introduces this degree of inflexibility, and I submit that the subamendment offered this evening does nothing to strengthen the first amendment offered. I would argue that flexibility is an essential element in the operation of the bill and that its removal would have a serious effect on the effectiveness of the bill.
I would hope that on reflection the House would decide to reject the subamendment offered this evening because it does nothing to strengthen an amendment which already, in my view, would weaken the effectiveness of the bill.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: That is a fatuous argument.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I wish to say I share the objective of this bill, which is to realize the ambition of a growing number of Canadians at last to live our own life. But we cannot achieve this objective unless to a much larger degree than Bill C-132 proposes we repatriate our economy and replace our branch plant status, a status which a generation ago replaced the old colonial way of life but replaced it with something not much better.
One of the tragedies of Canadian history has been the way in which Canadians have never been just Canadians. We began as a colony of France and so some of us were
November 13, 1973

French Canadians. Then we became a colony of Britain and some of us were British Canadians. A generation ago, at the end of World War II, we became increasingly a subsidiary of the United States economically, culturally and in our life style, and so we became American Canadians. But at last there is a significant movement across this country to become a true nation of our own and to be simply Canadian Canadians.
We cannot achieve this objective, however, unless we can demythologize the kind of myths that almost lulled our people to sleep. One example has been the myth that foreign investment equals capital inflow, that we must have great capital investment so that necessary foreign capital will come into this country. The reality is that according to a report of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, two-thirds of the money used in the transactions of foreign-owned companies comes from Canadian banks rather than from sources outside the country. For example, McGraw-Hill bought the Ryerson Publishing Company for $2 million with a Canadian bank loan; ITT bought AIMCO with a Canadian bank loan; the Export Development Corporation gives most of its loans to eight corporations, five of which are foreign-owned.
The second myth we must demythologize is that foreign investment means jobs, that we must have more and more foreign investment so that Canadians can gain employment. But we are now realizing that foreign investment can mean unemployment through foreign-dominated companies and unions often giving priority to production in other countries. We know, also, that it can mean a concentration in the development of natural resource industries and a lower priority to secondary industries where most of the jobs are to be found. It is a tragic fact that of all the industrialized countries of the world, Canada has the smallest percentage of its investment in secondary manufacturing.
The third myth that we must demythologize is that Canadians need foreign management and foreign technology in order to develop their industry. I think there was a certain validity in this claim at one time, a validity in that at one time Canadian companies required the kind of expertise and know-how that had to be imported, just as at one time I think it was necessary for the Canadian labour movement to have international unions for precisely the same reason. But we have moved beyond that need, I hope, in both instances, both in terms of industrial and commercial management and in terms of the direction of our union movement. Given the opportunity, surely this country now has the mental equipment and the practical experience to develop its own resources and to manage its own affairs.
It seems to me that we should be able to go beyond the limitations of Bill C-132, we should be able to demythologize the notions that have so gripped the thinking of many Canadians throughout this country and have too long made us accept a branch plant mentality. If we look at the Toronto Star of January 12, 1973, we find that 68 per cent of the people of this country, according to the survey published in that newspaper, believed that the government's foreign ownership policy was inadequate or very inadequate. Two-thirds of the people surveyed were dis-
Foreign Investment Review Act satisfied with the kind of direction they were receiving from this government, the direction presented in the legislation we are debating tonight.
According to the International Review of March, 1973, in reply to the question, "Is foreign ownership good or bad?", we find that those who believe it is bad rose from just 33 per cent in 1969 to 47 per cent in 1972; that is, just a third of the Canadians surveyed four years ago were discontented with foreign investment, but now the fraction is almost one-half. Se we have to be conscious of the fact that a growing number of Canadians want the goal which is surely the objective of this bill, but an objective that is realized only to a very limited degree by this legislation. I would hope that we would all see Bill C-132 as simply the beginning, the first step down a road that we hope will lead us to an objective which surely we should all share and support, the kind of objective that Canadians have now delayed too long in seeking.
For those reasons, it is possible for all of us to support the principle and the objective of this bill; but there are some points upon which I think criticism needs to be directed against it. The first of these is the assumption of the government that you can achieve this goal by passing a law which generally approves Canadian ownership, when what we need is not just legislation along this line but an economic policy that will give some assistance to Canadian business and industry striving to uphold Canadian ownership. It would be much more inspiring to parliament and to the public if this legislation could be accompanied by that kind of economic policy.
Tonight I would like to ask that the attention of the House be directed toward the need of Canadian business for much more assistance than it is now receiving from this government. I refer in particular to small business, the kind of business that generates jobs, the kind of business that is surely the backbone of the Canadian economy. The sad fact is that Canadian small business is now suffering as never before. According to the Toronto Star of February 13, 1973, 2,848 businesses that could be described as small businesses went into bankruptcy in the previous year. It was the worst record since 1942.
The reasons so many small businesses, those companies that have assets under $1 million, are having such a difficult time are such facts of life in Canada today as the exorbitant taxation imposed on business by the government, the unfair and unreasonable interference with business by the government, the shortage of capital under which so many small businesses suffer. For example, the small business loans administration of this country reports that under the Small Businesses Loans Act, in 1972 only $28,328,126 were advanced in such loans compared with $25,582,269 in 1961. There has been almost no advance in ten years in actual dollars, let alone in purchasing power.
The fact is that this government is simply not getting behind small businesses in Canada. No wonder so many of them found it impossible to survive. I stress this point for this reason, that it is not enough for us as legislators simply to say that business shall be Canadian. What we must do is to initiate and support policies that will make it more and more possible for Canadians to go into business and to stay in business. It is so often a sad fact that a

November 13, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act businessman today finds it too attractive to sell out, faced as he is by the many problems of keeping a company going: there are the problems of taxation, government interference, shortage of capital, labour difficulties, and the like. It is often much easier simply to look in the mirror one morning and say, "Why should I go on this way?" It is easier to pick up the telephone, call New York, Chicago or Detroit and say, "If you still want this business, come and get it." What we need, therefore, is to bring about an economic policy that will make Canada a much more attractive country in which to do business; and the great failure of this government is not simply in initiating inadequate legislation but, much more seriously, in bringing about inadequate policies.
Much has been said in this debate on the amendments proposed by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay). In the interests of federalism there has been a denigration of the rights of the provinces to participate in the repatriation of our economy, to have some voice in the decisions that are made, decisions affecting their lives. I find it very interesting that so many members, particularly those to my left, who have been so articulate in speaking about participatory democracy and the rights of individuals to participate in decisions that affect them, in this instance turn away from that principle and seem to be opposed to the provinces having some say in that which affects them.
I have been particularly intrigued by the reasoning of the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), who spoke with his usual power in criticism of this amendment, speaking in favour of federalism-I must say a federalism without precedent in the history of Canada, that is, a federalism that would ignore the rights of the provinces- but then going on to move his curious subamendment that would give the same rights to territories. It would seem that he reasoned that what was wrong for ten should suddenly be right for 12, and that something which was to be rejected when applied to the provinces should be accepted if applied to provinces plus territories. We welcome the subamendment and I would hope that, if it passes, its mover would be prepared to support the amendment as modified by it.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) has criticized the subamendment and the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Central Nova on the grounds that they do not do justice to the needs and desires of all provinces concerned. It would seem to me, on reading the amendment as proposed, that there is nothing in it which would prevent the federal government from consulting with any province and eliciting from any provincial government a report on how a proposed takeover would affect its economy and its life.
The amendment requires that the province in which a business is being carried on shall be consulted. It requires that the compatability with that province be considered. But it certainly does not prevent the federal government from carrying on consultation with any other province. It seems to me that the intention of this amendment is not in any way to minimize the leadership of the federal government but, rather, to assert what is a basic principle of

Canadian confederation, that the federal government and the provincial governments shall work together.
We look at Bill C-132 with some gratitude in so far as we all recognize the need for the Canadian Parliament to enact legislation that will put us on the road toward the repatriation of our economy. We can regret that it does not go further. We can regret that there is an inadequate economic policy accompanying it, making its objective that much more unrealizable. But we can still support it, I think perhaps because of the philosophy expressed in a certain saloon sign in the Klondike many years ago which said, "Don't shoot the piano player-he's doing the best he can." Neither should we shoot down this bill, in so far as it is going to achieve something and the minister, we think, is doing the best he can. Maybe he is doing the best he can in that this is the best bill he can get through his own caucus and cabinet, and we welcome it to that extent and support it to that extent.
But I want to say, in closing, that I would hope and earnestly plead that this legislation be not the last step this parliament is asked to take. May it be but the first, not the last step that we will take down the road we hope will lead us to an objective that a growing number of Canadians seek. And if we are to follow that road, surely the government must be prepared to give leadership- greater leadership than it has given in the past. In this regard, the government has been content simply to follow public opinion rather than to give it direction. Its record to a great extent has been an acceptance of the willingness to have this country sold out.
Our memories go back to the 1956 pipeline debate when we recognized the attitude of the Liberal government of that time putting resources into the hands of foreign investors, resources that certainly should have had Canadian ownership and control. Perhaps at one time this might have been justified. I would have to admit that probably nobody is innocent enough to be justified in throwing the first stone. But we cannot justify it any longer. No party, no government can justify continuing Canada in the direction it has been going since the end of the Second World War. Therefore I would hope that Bill C-132 would be supported generally, at least as a symbol of the way in which Canadian parliamentarians and the Canadian government are going to turn this trend around and to move in another direction.
So very frequently it has been the case that our leaders in government have wanted to say to the people, "Tell us where you want to go and let us lead you there." But we would hope that for once the government would be willing to point this country in the direction it should follow; that for once we could at least gain a fraction of the kind of faith, conviction and vision that made the founding of this country possible.
Just the other night I read this statement by A. R. M. Lower, an historian who surely should be respected by members on the other side of this House, commenting on historic developments just a few years after the beginning of confederation: "Confederation was kept alive only by the faith of its founders and the vision they had of a country yet to be developed." I think that across this country tonight there are millions of Canadians, especially young people, who have that kind of faith and that kind of
November 13, 1973

vision and who are looking to us to give them that kind of leadership.
Just a century ago Thomas D'Arcy McGee could speak of a new nationality. At the end of 100 years and more of confederation we can see that a new nationality has come into being. Yet it has not taken the full form that all of us could wish it might take. What we are seeking is a new sense of that nationality, a new awareness that we are neither colony nor subsidiary nor branch plant, but a nation whose people are masters of their fate and captains of their soul. And to achieve that we can look forward to a time when in the economy, as in the political and cultural life of this country, we will truly be living our own life.

Mr. Speaker, the subject of foreign ownership has been foremost in the minds of Canadians for the past several years, although in most people's minds, encouraged by the members of the NDP, it is American ownership rather than foreign ownership that concerns them. This concept is, of course, wrong and as Canadians we should be concerned about the inflow of any capital into our country whether it be from the United States of America, Germany, Britain, France, Japan or other country.
There is no question that foreign investment in our country has been increasing at a fairly rapid rate over the years. It is the effect that foreign investment has on our economy that is of concern to the public. We cannot really blame the foreign investors; we must blame ourselves. When the minister of finance for the province of Saskatchewan appeared before the Standing Committee of Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs on June 19, he said that foreign investors operating in Canada have until now simply operated by the rules of the game, and there is no reason why they should operate differently in the absence of adequate guidelines and controls by Canada.
As the problem is a national one, it is the responsibility of the federal government to enact the legislation necessary to minimize the effect of foreign ownership on our economy, and I emphasize the word "minimize". There is no question that foreign investment is necessary if Canada is to continue to develop as an industrial nation, but I believe it is the responsibility of parliament, as was said by a spokesman for the government of Ontario, "to ensure that future investments by foreign corporations make an effective contribution to the achievement of national economic and social objectives."
Quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, I was disappointed with this bill. All it does is allow a group of bureaucrats in Ottawa to make decisions with respect to foreign investment which affect every region and province of Canada, and this without consultation or input by the region or province. This bill is another example of the arrogance of the government in presenting legislation which affects every region and province in the dominion, without first having met with the provinces and come to a consensus. It is a bill which is politically motivated, a vote-catcher, because the subject of foreign ownership is on the lips of almost every concerned Canadian today.
Foreign Investment Review Act
That Canada is a country made up of economic and physical regions is a fact of life and has been since confederation. Every region, in fact every province, has its own problems and there is a great deal of regional disparity. Because of this we have a program such as DREE and, of course, we have equalization payments which are worked out every year to help the have-not provinces. Industrial development has been concentrated in central Canada over the years because the wealth of the country has been siphoned into the financial circles of Toronto and Montreal, there to be utilized in industrial development in the area immediately surrounding the cities.
It is granted that industry tends to concentrate where the markets are, in the areas of greatest density of population; but inequities in freight rates over the years, particularly between central Canada and the west, have tended to discourage industrial development even of a secondary nature. Only in recent years has there been any move toward developing industry on the Prairies, and this has primarily been due to foreign capital. As I said, Mr. Speaker, foreign capital is necessary, but there must be some means of controlling its use in a way that will effectively benefit Canada. I am very disappointed with this bill, and one of the reasons for that disappointment is lack of participation by the provinces or regions concerned in the decision-making.
When I attended the Western Economic Opportunities Conference in Calgary in July as an observer, I was told that the conference was the first occasion on which some of our top civil servants had visited western Canada and that they were amazed to find such a large and attractive city as Calgary out on the Prairies. I do not know how true that statement was, but it concerned me a great deal. What concerns me even more is that, if it is true, it is this type of person or possibly persons without any intimate knowledge of the economic and social needs of the area who will be sitting on the screening agency making recommendations on whether foreign capital should be allowed to come into the Prairies. The analogy applies equally to the Maritimes.
Notwithstanding what the hon. member for Timiskam-ing (Mr. Peters) said, Mr. Speaker, each province must have input with respect to applications by individuals or corporations who plan on making an investment in that province or region. In addition, a majority of the persons in the agency considering the application must represent the province or region where the applicant intends making the investment. Without this type of input and representation, the province will be at the mercy of Ottawa-and I feel that will tend to further the alienation which appears to be building between the outlying regions and central Canada.
We in this party believe in one Canada. In order to keep going ahead, it is important that major pieces of legislation such as this bill be acceptable to all provinces.
I see it is ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

November 13, 1973

subtopic: NORTHERN AFFAIRS-NORTHWEST TERRITORIES- ALLEGED LETTING OF CONTRACTS BY HIRE NORTH WITHOUT TENDERS
NORTHERN AFFAIRS-NORTHWEST TERRITORIES- ALLEGED LETTING OF CONTRACTS BY HIRE NORTH WITHOUT TENDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise again on this occasion to bring up the matter of apparent conflict of interest in the awarding of contracts for the Hire North program in the Northwest Territories. I very much like the concept of this program under which northern natives are hired to clear land for the Mackenzie Highway right-of-way and are trained to operate heavy equipment. This program, funded by the government of Canada and carried out by the government of the Northwest Territories, has provided native people with some of the direct economic benefit of the highway construction and with training and experience which may prove useful in future projects.
This program also has its dark side and it is of this side which, unfortunately, I feel I must speak tonight. It appears that the man hired to supervise and manage this project, Mr. Rudy Steiner, has awarded contracts of substantial value to firms, in which there is evidence to indicate he has an interest, without calling tenders. I have demanded that an appropriate committee of the House investigate this matter, and I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on Monday, November 5, in the absence of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien), whether he would agree to refer it. The Prime Minister answered that he had not understood my question and that he would read it when it appeared in Hansard. Mr. Speaker, I have submitted written questions on this matter because I want to see what information the government has in its possession, that it can treat this affair so flippantly.
I have information in my possession which warrants serious investigation, as do many thousands of newspaper readers across the country. I should like at this juncture to commend the reporters of the Edmonton Journal who have pursued this matter and who have delved alittlemore deeply into it than many reporters in this country are prone to delve. Let me share some of this information with the House. As the election approached last fall, the government was anxious to push ahead with land clearing for the Mackenzie highway. The Hire North program was to be a vehicle for this, and someone had to be found to manage the project who could get things done in a hurry. Accordingly, senior territorial officials approached Mr. Steiner who had a reputation for getting things done with a minimum of bureaucratic delay. He did away with a lot of bureaucratic delay all right; before he had even signed his own employment contract he had committed the government to expenses in excess of half a million dollars.

He was also responsible for awarding contracts in the amount of $227,110 without tender calls, and $46,700 with questionable tender calls, to two companies-Great Bear Industries Ltd. and Homes North. It was alleged that these were the only companies that could provide the equipment required in these contracts. But there are others who would like to have had a crack at them. Mr. Steiner co-signed a loan for Great Bear from the Canadian Acceptance Corporation on August 31, 1972, just two days after the firm was legally incorporated as a Northwest Territories company. This company received $124,560 in contracts.
Mr. Steiner was also at the time a director of Berg Insurance Agencies Ltd., of which Homes North is a division. Homes North received $154,920 in contracts, all without tenders. A number of contracts were also awarded to Cross Arctic Transport Ltd., of which Mr. Steiner is a director and major shareholder. At least he got the job done with a minimum of bureaucratic delay.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development knew about this, because he received a letter dated October 12, 1972, from Mr. Andre Carrell, office manager of Hire North at Fort Simpson, who felt he could not remain silent. His letter was sent back north to Stuart Hodgson, commissioner of the Northwest Territories, who asked deputy commissioner John Parker to investigate. Mr. Carrell, incidentally, is no longer employed in the Northwest Territories. In spite of these and other irregularities, of which the minister and top territorial officials are aware, Mr. Steiner is back on the job with Hire North.
I repeat my demand to the government, Mr. Speaker, that this matter be submitted to the Standing Committee on Public Accounts or to whatever committee is deemed appropriate. I am not after anyone's head and I do not wish to delay the Hire North project: I hope it is clear that this is not my intention. What is important, though, is that the people of the north be protected from this phony frontierism, from this disregard for the fundamental rules of fairness and honesty in awarding contracts. I respectfully await the response of the government.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few points in response to the hon. member. I assure him the government has nothing to hide in this regard. At some later point I would be happy to discuss this matter with the hon. member very fully, as would the minister at an appropriate time before the committee.
When this subject was first raised in the fall of 1972, it was investigated by the deputy commissioner of the Northwest Territories. The report supplied by the commissioner indicated the following points. First, although Mr. Steiner was a director of Berg Insurance, a parent of Homes North which company rented portable homes to Hire North, he had no financial interest in the company. He later resigned his directorship. Second, there appeared to be no connection between Mr. Steiner and Great Bear Industries Ltd. and no evidence of impropriety in Mr. Steiner's dealings with any of the companies supplying goods or equipment to the Hire North project.
November 13, 1973

Third, Mr. Steiner was authorized by the Northwest Territories government to rent portable camp buildings and other pieces of mobile equipment. Since companies normally supplying portable camp buildings could not meet the requirement in time, a purchase was negotiated. The total amount involved in these arrangements for portable camp buildings and mobile equipment amounted to $219,100. After the initial camps and equipment had been assembled late in August and early September, 1972, all further equipment required has been obtained through tendering procedures.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-ALLEGED RUG-RANKING SYSTEM OF PROMOTING SECRETARIES-REQUEST FOR SUBSTITUTION OF POINT RATING SYSTEM AND TABLING OF RELATIVE TREASURY BOARD MINUTES

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-ALLEGED RUG-RANKING SYSTEM OF PROMOTING SECRETARIES-REQUEST FOR SUBSTITUTION OF POINT RATING SYSTEM AND TABLING OF RELATIVE TREASURY BOARD MINUTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on July 23, 1973, as recorded at page 5870 of Hansard, I directed a question to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) with regard to a problem that has been rampant in the Public Service of Canada, namely, the practice of what is commonly called rug-ranking. I asked the minister whether he would consider replacing that unfair and discriminatory practice with a system which would provide for promotion by way of merit for secretaries in the public service. I asked this question particularly in view of the fact that other professional groups in the public service have enjoyed such assistance for more than a decade.
In his answer, the minister did not respond to the question put to him. I think what he said could properly be described as an impressive defence of the status quo. The purpose of the question was to secure recognition of the duties actually performed by secretaries in the public service. I want to point out that secretarial work was not always considered to be women's work. Despite opposition to women in the labour force, many women continued to seek and find employment in government service and elsewhere almost a century ago. In 1885, only 23 of more than 4,000 civil servants were women and one-third of these were third-class clerks-the lowest level-in the Post Office Department. But times have changed and women now make up an important part of the public service.
In 1970, the Royal Commission on the Status of Women made a special recommendation to the federal government with regard to the ST occupational group. In the chapter headed "Women in the Canadian economy," the commission stated that the present system of classifying STs, referred to as rug-ranking, seriously infringed on the rights of individuals to equitable treatment and placed secretaries in a position in which their pay was dependent on the pay received by others. The Royal Commission on the Status of Women echoed some earlier findings in a study made for the Public Service Commission. It went on to say:
The career structure of STs looks more like a steeple than a pyramid. This is attributable to rug-ranking which not only curtails opportunities for STs but means that lower level officers whose work requires a very good secretary either cannot get one, or, should they succeed in getting an exceptional stenographer, cannot treat her fairly, or increase the chances of her staying by
Adjournment Debate
rewarding her adequately. This form of linking of the fate of secretaries to the fate of their bosses has another interesting "hooker" in it; a woman of ST-6 level or higher may well find herself in a state of suspended animation should the boss leave the public service since the incoming boss will be inclined to promote his own secretary.
Lately, with full implementation of the Public Service Commission's bilingualism program and the realization that bilingual secretaries' quotas which once seemed safely far away are already looming on the horizon, the ST classification system has acquired still another "hooker". A number of recommendations have been made, and in my view they should be taken up by the government. First, with respect to the language question, there ought to be a standard testing system uniformly administered. A second language training course for secretaries should be developed and instituted by the language bureau. Increased access to French language training in all aspects, reading, writing and comprehension should be made possible.
These are not the end of the recommendations which have been made on the matter. I commend this brief to the government. With respect to the revision of the ST classification standard, may I say that approximately 15,000 employees are classified as STs in the administrative support category of the public service. The STs have the specialized skills of typing, working with dictaphones or taking shorthand dictation and transcribing it. Many of them have the added and demonstrated ability to perform as executive assistants to management executives. If the present system of rug-ranking is not curtailed, these latter abilities will not be allowed to flower.
A further recommendation which I pass on to the government is that as an alternative to rug-ranking, a point rating system be developed, that there be an immediate revaluation of the ST group and of ST positions, and that a full examination of promotion, training, career development and mobility opportunities be made. Another recommendation is as follows:
That the administrative and attitude barriers be removed that prevent STs from entering competitions for other categories.
The objective of the Public Service of Canada and all of those who perform services on behalf of the people of Canada for the Government of Canada and those of us that work in this chamber ought to be that the best and fairest system possible be applied; that a person be permitted to advance on his or her own merits. With respect to those in the ST categories, that facility and avenue is sadly lacking. I hope that as a result of this debate and the questions which preceded it, the government will take a long, serious and hard look at the problem of those who are caught in this dilemma.
